paragraphs: Atlantis NDT delivers 40-hour ET Level I training aligned to the ASNT body of knowledge and structured to satisfy both SNT-TC-1A written practices and NAS 410 formal-training requirements — one course, either destination. Employers get the full certification infrastructure from our ASNT Level III consultants: written practice development, examination administration with NAS 410-compliant question banks, vision programs, and audit-ready records. Affordable, accessible, fully customizable to your parts, probes, and procedures. Explore the method curriculum at /eddy-current-testing-training and the entry landscape at /ndt-level-1-training, then request a quote for a seat or a complete program.

faq.q: Do the 40 training hours satisfy both SNT-TC-1A and NAS 410?
faq.a: Yes, when the course outline covers the required body of knowledge — both systems specify 40 formal training hours for ET Level I/1. The difference is downstream: NAS 410 demands 400 experience hours, mandated exam minimums, and annual vision.

faq.q: Can prior electronics experience reduce my ET requirements?
faq.a: Under SNT-TC-1A, two years of engineering or science study can reduce classroom hours at the Level III's discretion, and documented prior training may be credited. NAS 410 credits documented previous training and experience but does not reduce its minimums.

faq.q: Is ET Level I certification portable?
faq.a: No — certification is employer-issued under both standards and ends with employment. Your training certificates and experience logs transfer, and NAS 410 shops accept documented prior hours; recertification with a new employer is fast when records are complete.

faq.q: What is the difference between NAS 410 and EN 4179?
faq.a: They are harmonized aerospace standards — NAS 410 from AIA for the US, EN 4179 for Europe — with closely aligned training, experience, and examination requirements. Multinational aerospace employers typically run one written practice satisfying both.

faq.q: Does ET Level I cover tube inspection?
faq.a: The fundamentals apply, but bobbin-coil tubing work is its own technique with dedicated procedures, and most written practices train and examine it specifically. Outage-season tubing crews typically pair Level I data collectors with Level II analysts who interpret the signals.

title: ET Level 2 Training: SNT-TC-1A vs NAS 410 Hours, Aerospace Path
description: ET Level II compared: SNT-TC-1A's 840 cumulative hours vs NAS 410's 1,200 for aerospace, impedance-plane interpretation authority, exam minimums, and US pay data.
h1: Eddy Current Testing Level II Training Requirements
answer: ET Level II under SNT-TC-1A requires 80 cumulative training hours (40 plus 40) and 840 cumulative experience hours (210 plus 630). Aerospace's NAS 410 keeps the 80 training hours but demands 1,200 experience hours for direct Level 2 — with a mandated 40-question general exam and annual vision checks. Level II holds interpretation authority: reading the impedance plane and dispositioning parts.
expansion: Eddy current Level II is where the aerospace demand story concentrates. Airframe and engine inspection is fatigue-crack detection around fasteners, bolt holes, and blade roots — work that only an interpreting Level II can disposition, and NAS 410's higher experience wall keeps qualified supply chronically short. The standards diverge exactly where it costs time: formal training is 40+40 hours under both systems, but SNT-TC-1A's cumulative 840 experience hours become 1,200 under NAS 410 for direct Level 2 (400 at Level 1 plus 800 more with prior Level 1 certification). NAS 410 also mandates exam minimums — 40 general questions, 30 specific — annual near-vision and color perception checks, and Responsible Level 3 approval of the program. General industry keeps its own Level II market in heat-exchanger tubing analysis. Method fundamentals are at /eddy-current-testing-training, the cross-method Level II view at /ndt-level-2-training, and full hour tables at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method.

facets.q: Why does NAS 410 require more experience hours than SNT-TC-1A?
facets.a: Aerospace eddy current findings disposition fatigue-critical hardware — engine disks, wing attachments, bolt holes — where a missed crack is catastrophic. NAS 410 is a minimum standard with 'shall' language, and its 1,200-hour direct Level 2 wall buys judgment that classroom hours cannot.

facets.q: What does an ET Level II do that a Level I cannot?
facets.a: Set up and standardize equipment from scratch, choose frequencies and probes within procedure limits, interpret impedance-plane signals — separating cracks from lift-off, edge effect, and permeability noise — accept or reject parts, document dispositions, and supervise Level I technicians and trainees.

facets.q: How long does it take to reach ET Level II in aerospace?
facets.a: With NAS 410's 1,200 experience hours, a full-time trainee needs roughly seven to nine months of logged method time plus 80 training hours and exams — most candidates land certification in about a year. The SNT-TC-1A route at 840 hours runs a few months faster.

facets.q: Is heat-exchanger tubing analysis a Level II job?
facets.a: Yes — bobbin and array tubing data analysis is a classic SNT-TC-1A Level II role. Outage crews collect terabytes of coil data; certified analysts interpret signals, size wall loss, and disposition tubes, often remotely from the data they are fed.

facets.q: Do aerospace employers accept SNT-TC-1A ET Level II?
facets.a: Generally no. Primes and their supply chains flow down NAS 410 or EN 4179 contractually. Your training and logged hours carry over, but the employer must certify you under its NAS 410 written practice, including its mandated exams and annual vision.

facets.q: What surface techniques does aerospace ET Level II cover?
facets.a: Pencil-probe scanning around fastener heads and radii, automated rotary bolt-hole inspection, conductivity verification for alloy and heat-treat condition, and increasingly eddy current array for coverage-critical surfaces — each standardized on reference standards with EDM notches.

sections.heading: The two hour-stacks, side by side
paragraphs: Formal training is identical under both systems: 40 hours at Level I plus 40 at Level II, 80 cumulative. Experience is where the standards split. SNT-TC-1A recommends 210 plus 630 hours — 840 cumulative in the method. NAS 410 requires 400 hours at Level 1 and 800 more for Level 2 with prior Level 1 certification, or 1,200 hours for direct Level 2 — roughly 40 percent more time on hardware than general industry. The gap is deliberate: NAS 410 is a minimum standard whose numbers cannot be reduced by any written practice, where SNT-TC-1A's table is a recommendation employers adapt. Plan your timeline against the standard your target industry actually uses; the tables for every method are at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method.

sections.heading: Interpretation authority: the impedance plane is the job
paragraphs: An ET Level II's defining skill is reading the impedance plane — the two-dimensional display where every signal is a vector whose phase and amplitude encode what caused it. Lift-off sweeps one direction; conductivity change another; a surface crack breaks the eddy current flow with a phase signature that deepens predictably with flaw depth. The Level II separates these in real time, on parts where edge effect, fastener geometry, and permeability noise all crowd the screen. Under both standards, that judgment carries disposition authority: accept, reject, document, and defend. It is also why the experience walls exist — phase discrimination is pattern recognition, and pattern recognition is built only from hours of standardized, supervised looking.

sections.heading: Why aerospace demand concentrates at ET Level II
paragraphs: Aerospace is the largest eddy current employer because the method is unmatched for surface and near-surface fatigue cracks in conductive alloys — exactly the failure mode that governs aircraft structures. Airframe programs inspect fastener holes and skin around them; engine shops inspect disk bores, blade roots, and dovetails; MRO stations re-inspect on every heavy check. All of it requires an interpreting Level II under a NAS 410 or EN 4179 written practice, and the 1,200-hour experience wall means supply cannot surge when demand does. The result is a persistent seller's market for certified aerospace ET Level IIs, concentrated around US aerospace hubs — Wichita, the Puget Sound, Connecticut's engine corridor, and the Texas and Florida MRO belts.

sections.heading: The general-industry Level II market: tubing analysis
paragraphs: Outside aerospace, the strongest ET Level II demand is heat-exchanger and condenser tubing inspection in power and process plants. Bobbin coils fly through thousands of tubes per outage shift, generating data that a certified analyst must interpret: distinguishing wall loss, pitting, and cracking from support-plate signals and deposits, sizing indications in percent through-wall, and dispositioning tubes for plugging. This is SNT-TC-1A territory — 840 cumulative hours — and it is one of the few NDT roles that can be performed substantially off-site, since analysis happens on recorded data. Nuclear plants layer additional qualification requirements on top, making experienced tubing analysts among the best-compensated Level IIs in general industry.

sections.heading: Exams under both standards — and where candidates fail
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A prescribes the familiar trio — general, specific, practical — at a recommended 80 percent composite, with content set by the written practice. NAS 410 hardens the structure: the general exam shall contain at least 40 questions, closed-book; the specific at least 30, covering the employer's specifications and techniques; and the practical is a proficiency demonstration on representative hardware, from setup and standardization through scan, interpretation, and documentation. Failure patterns are consistent across both systems: candidates pass the written exams and stumble on practical interpretation — misreading phase on a bolt-hole standard, or failing to re-verify standardization after a probe change. NAS 410 additionally requires documented remedial training before any re-examination.

sections.heading: Vision requirements: annual, and stricter in aerospace
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A's regime — annual near-vision at Jaeger No. 2 or equivalent from not less than 12 inches, color-contrast differentiation at intervals not exceeding five years — is the general-industry baseline. NAS 410 requires near vision and color perception verified annually for every certified level, no five-year color cycle. For eddy current the color requirement is functional, not formal: modern instruments encode channels and alarm states in color, and array systems paint C-scans in graded palettes. Lapsed vision exams suspend certification immediately under both systems, and aerospace auditors check vision records with the same rigor as exam scores — an easily avoided finding that shows up in real audits constantly.

sections.heading: What ET Level II pays in the US
paragraphs: ZipRecruiter's NDT Level 2 band runs $48,000 to $90,000 with top earners above it, and the BLS median for all nondestructive testing specialists sits at $78,350 (May 2025). Aerospace ET Level IIs cluster in the upper half of that range: NAS 410's experience wall restricts supply, and primes pay for it — with engine-shop and nuclear tubing-analysis roles at the top of the method. Multi-technique holders (surface, bolt-hole rotary, array, tubing) out-earn single-technique peers consistently. US-first bands by method, industry, and region — including how aerospace ET compares against pipeline RT and PAUT premiums — are maintained at /blog/ndt-salary-guide-2026-global.

sections.heading: Routes to ET Level II: ladder, direct, and crossover
paragraphs: Three routes lead here. The ladder route certifies Level I first — 40 hours training, 210 or 400 experience hours by standard — then adds the second 40-hour course and remaining hours. The direct route runs the full stack as a documented trainee: 80 training and 840 hours under SNT-TC-1A, or 1,200 under NAS 410, then examines straight to Level II. The crossover route brings a certified ET Level II across the standards boundary — general industry to aerospace or back — carrying training certificates and logged hours but requiring full re-examination under the new employer's written practice, including NAS 410's mandated minimums and annual vision when moving toward aerospace. Complete personal records make every route faster.

sections.heading: Training ET Level II with Atlantis
paragraphs: Atlantis NDT's 40-hour ET Level II course is built around interpretation: impedance-plane analysis drills, phase-depth discrimination on EDM-notched standards, bolt-hole and surface-scan practicals, and tubing-signal fundamentals — structured to satisfy SNT-TC-1A written practices and NAS 410 formal-training requirements alike. For employers, our ASNT Level III consultants deliver the full program: NAS 410-compliant written practices with Responsible Level 3 review, examination banks meeting the 40/30 question minimums, annual vision tracking, and audit-ready records. Affordable, accessible, fully customizable to your hardware and specifications. Start from /eddy-current-testing-training and /ndt-level-2-training, then request a quote for seats or a complete certification program.

faq.q: Can I certify directly to ET Level II without holding Level I?
faq.a: Yes, under both standards. SNT-TC-1A requires the summed hours — 80 training, 840 experience. NAS 410 permits direct Level 2 at 80 training hours and 1,200 experience hours, all logged as a documented trainee under qualified supervision before examination.

faq.q: Do my SNT-TC-1A hours count toward NAS 410 certification?
faq.a: Documented training and experience hours carry over — NAS 410 accepts verifiable prior records. But the new employer must still examine and certify you under its NAS 410 written practice, meeting the mandated exam minimums and annual vision requirements in full.

faq.q: Is eddy current array a separate certification from ET Level II?
faq.a: Typically an additional technique qualification on top of conventional ET Level II, with supplemental training and practical examination defined in the written practice — parallel to how PAUT sits atop conventional UT. Array-qualified Level IIs command a premium.

faq.q: How often must an aerospace ET Level II recertify?
faq.a: NAS 410 sets a five-year maximum recertification interval, with annual vision exams throughout and refresher training triggered by gaps — including any 12-month lapse between training and certification, or extended interruption of method work.

faq.q: What should I study for the ET Level II general exam?
faq.a: Impedance-plane theory, phase-depth relationships, skin depth and frequency selection, probe types and field patterns, standardization discipline, and signal discrimination — cracks versus lift-off, edge, and permeability effects. Under NAS 410, expect at least 40 closed-book questions across that span.

title: MT Level 1 Training: 12 Hours Class, 70 Hours OJT (SNT-TC-1A)
description: SNT-TC-1A recommends 12 classroom hours and 70 hours of MT experience for Level I. What the exams cover, what Level I may do on the job, and how to get certified.
h1: Magnetic Particle Testing Level I: Requirements, Exams, and What the Cert Lets You Do
answer: MT Level I certification under SNT-TC-1A requires 12 hours of formal classroom training, 70 hours of work experience in magnetic particle testing, and 130 total NDT hours. You then pass three employer-administered exams — general, specific, and practical — plus an annual near-vision test and a color-contrast test. Your employer, not ASNT, issues the certification against its written practice.
expansion: The 12-hour classroom figure surprises people: it is triple the 4 hours required for PT Level I, because magnetic particle testing carries real physics — field direction, circular versus longitudinal magnetization, AC versus DC penetration — that the trainee must apply before touching a part. The 70 method hours and 130 total NDT hours are on-the-job experience, logged under supervision, and they are what actually gates most candidates: a full-time trainee typically accumulates them in a few weeks to a few months depending on how much MT work the shop runs. Because SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice, your employer's written practice sets the final numbers, and it may raise them. A Level I performs magnetization, particle application, and recording per written instructions; interpretation and accept/reject decisions stay with Level II. Full per-method figures are in our training hours guide.
source: SNT-TC-1A (2024 ed.) recommended training and experience table; ASTM E709; employer written practice requirements per SNT-TC-1A Section 9

facets.q: How many training hours does MT Level 1 require?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A recommends 12 hours of formal classroom training for MT Level I, plus 70 hours of work experience in magnetic particle testing and 130 total NDT hours. Your employer's written practice sets the binding numbers and may exceed these.

facets.q: Can an MT Level 1 accept or reject parts?
facets.a: No. A Level I performs setups, magnetization, particle application, and recording per written instructions. Interpretation of indications and accept/reject decisions require Level II or III. A Level I who signs off welds is operating outside SNT-TC-1A.

facets.q: Does ASNT issue MT Level 1 certification?
facets.a: No. Under SNT-TC-1A, your employer certifies you against its written practice after training, experience, exams, and vision checks. ASNT publishes the recommended practice; central ASNT certification exists mainly at Level III and via the ASNT NDT Level II program.

facets.q: How long does it take to become MT Level 1?
facets.a: The classroom portion is 12 hours — typically 2 to 3 training days. The gating item is 70 hours of supervised MT experience plus 130 total NDT hours, which a full-time trainee in a busy shop can log in roughly three to six weeks.

facets.q: What vision tests does MT Level 1 require?
facets.a: An annual near-vision acuity exam — Jaeger 2 or equivalent at not less than 12 inches, corrected or uncorrected — plus a color/shade differentiation test. Fluorescent MT work makes the color test consequential, not a formality.

facets.q: Is MT Level 1 worth it without other methods?
facets.a: Rarely on its own. US employers almost always certify surface-method techs in MT and PT together, often adding VT. The three combined cost little extra classroom time and make you dispatchable to far more jobs.

sections.heading: What an MT Level I is certified to do — and what stays off-limits
paragraphs: An MT Level I performs magnetic particle examinations per written instructions: setting up the yoke or bench unit, verifying it with a lift check, magnetizing the part in the required directions, applying dry or wet particles, and recording what appears. Under SNT-TC-1A, all of it happens under the supervision of a certified Level II or Level III. The Level I is the hands of the operation — a competent one keeps a crew productive by handling the physical workflow reliably.

What the Level I explicitly does not do is interpret. Deciding whether an indication is relevant, whether a relevant indication is rejectable under the governing code, and what goes on the report — that authority belongs to Level II and above. This division is not bureaucratic caution; a linear indication at a weld toe can be a toe crack or harmless magnetic writing, and telling them apart is exactly the judgment the Level II exam tests.

For employers, this means an MT Level I cannot be sent out alone to inspect and disposition work. If a contract requires MT with signed accept/reject results, at least one Level II must be on the job. If you are hiring for a solo field role, you need our MT Level II page, not this one.

sections.heading: The SNT-TC-1A numbers: 12 classroom hours, 70 method hours, 130 total
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A's recommended initial qualification for MT Level I is 12 hours of formal training, 70 hours of work experience in the MT method, and 130 hours of total NDT experience. The total-experience figure means hours logged in other methods — PT, VT — count toward the 130, which is why surface-method trainees typically qualify in multiple methods on overlapping timelines.

Two structural details matter. First, SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice: your employer's written practice adopts, and may raise, these numbers, and the written practice is the legally binding document auditors check. Second, the training-hour footnotes allow reductions for candidates with relevant post-secondary education in engineering or science — a degreed candidate may sit fewer classroom hours at the employer's discretion.

Candidates can also certify directly to Level II without holding Level I, but the hours stack: 20 classroom hours, 280 MT hours, and 530 total NDT hours combined. Nothing is skipped — the Level I requirements are absorbed into the Level II gate. The full per-method, per-level table is in our NDT training hours guide at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method, and the national method page at /magnetic-particle-testing-training covers the method beyond Level I.

sections.heading: Why MT asks for triple the classroom time of PT
paragraphs: PT Level I needs 4 classroom hours; MT Level I needs 12. The difference is physics. Penetrant testing works the same way on every part; magnetic particle results depend entirely on whether you put a field of adequate strength in the right direction through the right volume of material. A discontinuity shows only when it interrupts flux — meaning it must lie roughly perpendicular to the field. Magnetize in one direction only and you are blind to half the cracks.

So the 12 hours cover circular versus longitudinal magnetization, why every part needs examination in two perpendicular directions, and how technique choices change what you can find. AC current concentrates flux at the surface — ideal for surface fatigue cracks; half-wave DC drives deeper for near-surface discontinuities in castings and weldments. Yokes induce longitudinal fields between poles; prods and central conductors produce circular fields; coils wrap longitudinal fields around shafts and axles.

A Level I is not choosing techniques — the written instruction does that. But the operator must understand field direction well enough to position a yoke correctly, recognize when coverage overlap is inadequate, and know why the instruction demands two orientations. That comprehension is what the general exam probes, and it is where self-taught candidates fail.

sections.heading: The three exams and the 70/80 grading rule
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A qualification uses three exams. The general exam is written and closed-book, covering MT fundamentals: magnetism, current types, particle systems, demagnetization. The specific exam is also written but targets your employer's equipment, written practice, and the codes and procedures you will actually work under — a shop doing structural weld MT writes a different specific exam than an aerospace overhaul facility.

The practical exam is hands-on. The candidate demonstrates the full examination sequence on representative test samples with known discontinuities, graded by a Level III or designee against a documented checklist: equipment checks, technique execution, particle application, and correct recording of what the samples show. For Level I, the practical proves you can execute an instruction faithfully — not that you can disposition results.

Grading follows the standard SNT-TC-1A rule: minimum 70% on each individual exam and a composite average of at least 80% across the three. Failing one exam typically means retesting that exam after additional training, with the retest terms set by the written practice.

sections.heading: Vision requirements: the annual test with real teeth in MT
paragraphs: Every SNT-TC-1A certificate holder needs an annual near-vision examination — Jaeger 2 or equivalent characters read at not less than 12 inches, with corrected vision acceptable — plus a color and shade differentiation test. In some methods the color test feels like a formality. In MT it is not.

Fluorescent MT, the dominant technique in bench and aerospace work, produces green-yellow indications against a dark background under UV-A light. Visible dry-powder work relies on contrast between particle color and part surface. An examiner with a red-green color deficiency may genuinely struggle to detect or discriminate indications, which is why written practices treat the color-differentiation result seriously and some employers screen for it before investing in training.

Practical advice for candidates: take the vision exam before you book training. It costs little, any occupational clinic or optometrist can administer the Jaeger and Ishihara-type tests, and discovering a disqualifying deficiency after 12 classroom hours and weeks of OJT is an expensive way to learn it.

sections.heading: Equipment and consumables you will train on
paragraphs: Field MT in the US runs mostly on portable electromagnetic yokes. You will learn the dead-weight lift check that verifies magnetizing capability: an AC yoke must lift at least 10 pounds, a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds at 2-to-4-inch pole spacing, per ASTM E709 and ASME Section V. That check happens at required intervals and gets logged — a failed lift check invalidates work done since the last good one.

Bench work introduces wet-horizontal units: head and tail stocks for circular magnetization through the part, coils for longitudinal fields, and fluorescent particle baths whose concentration you verify with a settling test. You will also handle dry visible powders for hot or rough field surfaces, contrast paint for dark parts, and field indicators such as the pie gauge used to confirm field direction and adequacy.

Demagnetization closes the loop. Residual magnetism interferes with downstream machining, welding, and instrumentation, so Level I training covers AC coil demag and verifying residual field with a field indicator. It is an unglamorous step that shops fail audits over, and a Level I who does it right every time is worth keeping.

sections.heading: Who hires MT Level I techs in the US
paragraphs: The biggest steady employers are structural steel fabricators working to AWS D1.1, where MT is the standard surface examination on welds; oil and gas inspection contractors running MT on piping, tanks, and pressure vessels; and forging, casting, and machining operations doing in-process MT on components. Lifting-gear and crane inspection companies also run continuous MT programs on hooks, shackles, and spreader bars.

Be realistic about how the entry works: companies rarely post 'MT Level I' jobs. They hire NDT trainees or helpers, put them through training, and certify them as Level I once hours accrue — usually in MT and PT together, since the methods share job sites and the combined classroom load is small. Arriving with the 12 classroom hours already completed and documented makes you a cheaper, faster hire than a cold applicant.

Level I is a wage tier, not a destination: the market pays meaningfully more at Level II, where you can work unsupervised and sign results, and more again when you stack UT. For current US pay bands by method and level, see the salary guide at /blog/ndt-salary-guide-2026-global — and note our finding that multi-method surface techs out-earn single-method peers at the same level.

sections.heading: How to get certified — and how Atlantis runs MT Level I training
paragraphs: The path in order: complete a 12-hour MT Level I course with documented outline and hours; log 70 MT hours and 130 total NDT hours under supervision; pass an employer-administered general, specific, and practical exam; pass the vision exams; receive certification from your employer against its written practice. If your employer lacks a written practice or a Level III to administer exams, that is a service gap an outside Level III fills — Atlantis provides exactly that as outsourced Level III consulting.

Atlantis delivers MT Level I training aligned to SNT-TC-1A hour and content recommendations, with exam banks and practical checklists your Level III can adopt directly, and hands-on time on yokes and wet bench units. We train at your facility or ours, and the same engagement can cover PT and VT Level I so one training window certifies a complete surface-method tech. Affordable, accessible, fully customizable — request a quote and we will scope it to your written practice.

Where to go next: the method overview at /magnetic-particle-testing-training, the level overview at /ndt-level-2-training for what comes after, the hour tables at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method, and our /mt-level-2-training page for the interpretation authority this certification leads to.

faq.q: Can I take MT Level 1 training online?
faq.a: The classroom portion can be delivered online or in a hybrid format under most written practices, but the practical skills — yoke handling, lift checks, particle application, bench operation — and the hands-on practical exam require physical equipment. Expect any credible program to include an in-person practical component.

faq.q: Do my MT Level 1 hours transfer to a new employer?
faq.a: Your documented training hours and experience records transfer; the certification itself does not. A new employer must certify you under its own written practice, though it can accept your documented training and experience and re-examine you rather than starting from zero. Keep copies of every training certificate and experience log.

faq.q: What is the difference between SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 for MT Level 1?
faq.a: SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice the employer may tailor; ANSI/ASNT CP-189 is a standard with mandatory minimums, required for some aerospace and defense work. The MT Level I hour structure is similar, but CP-189 removes the employer's discretion to reduce requirements. Your contract or customer spec dictates which applies.

faq.q: How much does MT Level 1 certification cost?
faq.a: Because certification is employer-issued, there is no ASNT certification fee at Level I. Costs are course tuition, examiner time, and vision exams — figures that vary by provider and format. Atlantis quotes MT Level I training on request, scoped to your written practice and group size.

faq.q: Is 70 hours of MT experience enough to actually be competent?
faq.a: It is enough to execute instructions reliably, which is what Level I certifies — it is deliberately not interpretation competence. SNT-TC-1A's structure assumes the Level I keeps learning under supervision toward the 280 cumulative method hours a Level II needs. Employers who treat freshly-certified Level Is as finished products misread the system.

title: MT Level 2 Training: Hours, Exams, and AWS D1.1 Sign-Off Authority
description: MT Level II adds 8 classroom hours and 210 method hours, plus accept/reject authority. AWS D1.1 structural work, yoke lift checks, exam content, and US demand.
h1: Magnetic Particle Level II: The Certification That Signs Structural Steel
answer: MT Level II under SNT-TC-1A requires 8 additional classroom hours beyond Level I (20 cumulative) and 210 more hours of MT experience (280 cumulative, 530 total NDT hours). Level II adds the authority Level I lacks: interpreting indications, accepting or rejecting to code, writing and signing reports, and supervising trainees. On AWS D1.1 structural work, MT results must be dispositioned by a Level II or III.
expansion: The classroom increment is small — most of the theory was front-loaded into MT Level I's 12 hours — but the experience jump is threefold, and that is deliberate. Level II certifies judgment: distinguishing a toe crack from magnetic writing, a subsurface indication from a permeability change, a rejectable linear indication from an acceptable one under the governing acceptance criteria. AWS D1.1, the dominant structural welding code in the US, requires NDT personnel qualified to SNT-TC-1A, with examinations performed by Level II technicians or by Level I working under a Level II — so the Level II is the person whose signature closes out MT on building and bridge steel. Fabricators pursuing or holding AISC certification, and DOT bridge shops, staff to that requirement. The employer still issues the certification against its written practice; the exams get harder and the practical adds flaw disposition and report writing. Hour tables for every method are at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method.
source: SNT-TC-1A (2024 ed.) recommended training and experience table; AWS D1.1 Structural Welding Code — Steel; ASTM E709

facets.q: How many hours do I need for MT Level 2?
facets.a: Beyond Level I: 8 more classroom hours and 210 more MT experience hours. Cumulative from zero: 20 classroom hours, 280 hours in MT, and 530 total NDT hours. The experience requirement, not the classroom, is what takes months.

facets.q: Can MT Level 2 techs work unsupervised?
facets.a: Yes. Level II is the first level authorized to independently set up, examine, interpret, accept or reject to the governing code, and sign the report. This is why solo field MT assignments and most job postings specify Level II as the minimum.

facets.q: What does AWS D1.1 require for MT personnel?
facets.a: D1.1 requires NDT personnel qualified per ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with examinations performed by Level II individuals — or Level I working under direct Level II supervision. Disposition of MT results on structural welds rests with the Level II or III.

facets.q: What is on the MT Level 2 exam?
facets.a: A deeper general exam (field theory, current selection, technique limitations), a specific exam on your employer's procedures and governing codes such as D1.1, and a practical where you examine seeded samples, classify indications, disposition them against acceptance criteria, and write the report.

facets.q: How long does Level I to Level II progression take?
facets.a: The 210 additional MT hours translate to roughly two to four months of full-time MT-heavy work, longer in shops where MT is intermittent. Many employers run the Level II classroom hours mid-progression so the exam follows soon after the hours complete.

facets.q: Do I also need a CWI for D1.1 MT work?
facets.a: No. The CWI covers visual inspection duties under D1.1; MT is an NDT function governed by the SNT-TC-1A qualification. Shops often employ both, and a Level II who later adds a CWI becomes significantly more valuable, but the MT sign-off requires the Level II, not the CWI.

sections.heading: What actually changes at Level II: authority, not technique
paragraphs: A good MT Level I already runs the yoke, the bench, and the particle systems competently. What Level II adds is everything downstream of the indication: deciding whether it is relevant, evaluating it against the governing acceptance criteria, accepting or rejecting the part or weld, writing the report, and signing it. Level II is also the first level authorized to supervise — which matters commercially, because one Level II can legitimize the output of several Level Is on a large job.

SNT-TC-1A frames this as the Level II being 'thoroughly familiar with the scope and limitations' of the method. In practice it means owning the failure modes: knowing that a field in only one direction misses transverse cracks, that an over-magnetized part throws false indications at geometry changes, that a lift check done wrong invalidates a shift's work. The Level II is accountable for results a Level I merely produces.

That accountability is why the experience requirement triples while the classroom barely grows. Interpretation is pattern recognition built on volume — hundreds of hours of real indications, geometry effects, and surface conditions. No 8-hour class substitutes for it, and SNT-TC-1A does not pretend otherwise.

sections.heading: The numbers: +8 classroom hours, +210 method hours
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A recommends 8 additional hours of formal training for MT Level II, on top of Level I's 12 — 20 cumulative. Experience is the real gate: 210 additional hours in MT beyond Level I's 70, for 280 cumulative in the method, within 530 total NDT hours. A candidate certifying directly to Level II without a Level I interval must present the combined totals.

Notice the asymmetry against other methods: MT Level II's method-experience requirement (210 additional) is substantially higher than PT's or VT's (140 each). The committee's logic is visible — MT interpretation involves more variables: field direction, current type, technique, part geometry, and permeability all shape what appears, so more supervised repetitions are demanded before you judge independently.

As always under SNT-TC-1A, your employer's written practice states the binding figures and may exceed these. Auditors — AISC, customer source inspectors, DOT — check your records against the written practice, not against the ASNT book. Complete per-method tables live at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method; the method fundamentals are at /magnetic-particle-testing-training and the level overview at /ndt-level-2-training.

sections.heading: Where AWS D1.1 puts the MT Level II
paragraphs: AWS D1.1 is the code most US structural steel is fabricated and erected under, and it requires NDT personnel qualified in accordance with SNT-TC-1A. Examinations are performed by Level II technicians, or by Level I techs working under the direct supervision of a Level II — and the disposition of results belongs to the Level II or III. When a fabricator's contract documents call for MT on fracture-critical welds, moment connections, or repaired areas, a Level II signature is what closes the item.

This creates concentrated, durable demand. AISC-certified fabricators must demonstrate qualified NDT capability, whether in-house or subcontracted. State DOT bridge programs layer additional requirements onto D1.5 work, and fracture-critical fabrication effectively mandates continuous surface examination coverage. Erection contractors need Level IIs for field MT on welded connections, often on night shifts and at height.

The D1.1 context also shapes technique. Structural work is mostly AC yoke with dry visible powder — fast, portable, effective on surface-breaking flaws in as-welded surfaces. The Level II decides when conditions justify deviation: wet fluorescent for critical or smooth-ground welds, half-wave DC where slightly subsurface detection is wanted, contrast paint on dark mill-scale surfaces.

sections.heading: Technique control: lift checks, prods, and the details audits catch
paragraphs: The Level II owns equipment verification. Yoke lift checks — 10 pounds for AC, 40 pounds for DC at 2-to-4-inch pole spacing per ASTM E709 — must be performed at the intervals the procedure requires and documented. A failed check does not just stop work; it throws every examination since the last good check into question, and the Level II decides the re-examination scope. Auditors read lift-check logs precisely because they are easy to neglect.

Prods put current directly through the part to generate circular fields — powerful on large weldments, but they arc-burn the surface if contact is poor, and arc strikes on structural steel are themselves rejectable conditions that can crack. Many structural contracts and owner specs restrict or prohibit prods on finished work. The Level II must know both the technique and where the contract forbids it.

Coverage is the other silent failure. Every area requires examination in two roughly perpendicular field directions, with overlap between yoke placements. On a long stiffener weld that means a disciplined placement pattern, not freestyle. Level II practical exams increasingly test exactly this: candidates who find the seeded flaw but leave coverage gaps fail.

sections.heading: Interpretation: relevant, non-relevant, and false indications
paragraphs: The core Level II skill is classification. False indications come from over-magnetization, surface roughness, or particle drainage patterns and vanish on re-examination with corrected technique. Non-relevant indications are real magnetic responses caused by geometry — section changes, drilled holes, the boundary of a heat-affected zone, magnetic writing from part-to-part contact — not by discontinuities. Relevant indications come from actual discontinuities and must be evaluated against acceptance criteria.

At a weld toe, the discrimination gets consequential. A tight toe crack, undercut filled with particles, and a permeability line at the fusion boundary can all present as linear indications in similar locations. The Level II's tools are re-examination at reduced field strength, light surface conditioning where permitted, orientation logic — cracks interrupt flux, permeability effects follow metallurgy — and experience with how each presents.

Then comes evaluation: applying the governing criteria to relevant indications. Under D1.1-referenced criteria, disposition depends on indication type, length, and the weld's loading category. The Level II must know which edition and which contract-modified criteria apply — a technician applying memorized limits from a previous job to a new contract is a documented, recurring cause of nonconformance.

sections.heading: The Level II exams: what your Level III will test
paragraphs: The general exam goes beyond Level I recall into applied theory: selecting current type and technique for a given part and flaw orientation, field-strength adequacy, demagnetization strategy, and the method's limitations — what MT cannot find, such as deep subsurface flaws or discontinuities parallel to the field. Expect calculation-style questions on coil and prod amperage rules.

The specific exam is built from your employer's written practice, procedures, and the codes on its contracts — for structural shops, that means D1.1 acceptance criteria, technique restrictions, and documentation requirements. The practical exam is the heart of Level II qualification: examine samples with seeded and incidental discontinuities, classify every indication, disposition the relevant ones against stated criteria, and produce a report a customer could audit. Grading follows the 70% minimum per exam, 80% composite rule.

Recertification runs on the interval your written practice sets — commonly three years for Level II, with annual vision exams throughout. Continuity matters: significant interruption in method work can trigger re-examination requirements, so document your hours continuously, not retroactively.

sections.heading: Demand and pay: what MT Level II is worth in the US market
paragraphs: Standing demand comes from structural fabrication shops, bridge fabricators, erection contractors, energy-sector inspection companies, and OEM component manufacturers. MT Level II rarely travels alone in job postings: the standard US surface-tech package is MT II + PT II, frequently with VT II attached, because the same technician covers all three on a site visit and the incremental certification cost is small.

On pay: surface-method Level IIs occupy the entry-professional band of NDT compensation — solidly above trainee wages, below UT and advanced-method rates. The premium moves when you stack methods and codes: an MT/PT/VT Level II who can work D1.1 jobs independently, and who later adds UT or a CWI, climbs into the upper technician bands. Current US figures by method, level, and sector are maintained in our salary guide at /blog/ndt-salary-guide-2026-global.

For employers, the calculus is different: a certified Level II converts subcontracted NDT spend into in-house capability and removes the scheduling dependency on outside crews — often the decisive argument for training up an existing Level I rather than hiring.

sections.heading: Getting to Level II with Atlantis
paragraphs: Atlantis runs MT Level II training built to SNT-TC-1A hour and topic recommendations, with D1.1-context interpretation practice on flawed weld samples, exam banks for general and specific exams, and practical checklists your Level III can adopt. If you have no in-house Level III, our outsourced ASNT Level III consulting administers the exams, maintains your written practice, and issues the supporting documentation — the complete employer-certification apparatus, provided as a service.

Training runs at your facility or ours, and pairs naturally with PT Level II and VT Level II in a single engagement for shops building a full surface-method bench. Affordable, accessible, fully customizable — request a quote and we will scope hours, samples, and exam administration to your written practice and contract requirements.

faq.q: Can I go straight to MT Level 2 without Level 1?
faq.a: Yes — SNT-TC-1A permits direct Level II certification if you present the combined requirements: 20 classroom hours, 280 hours of MT experience, and 530 total NDT hours, then pass the Level II exams. Experienced techs changing employers or documenting prior uncertified experience use this route routinely.

faq.q: Does MT Level 2 qualify me for both bench and field work?
faq.a: The certification covers the method, but your specific exam and practical reflect your employer's techniques. A written practice can limit certification scope — for example, yoke-only. Moving from structural yoke work to wet-bench aerospace MT typically means supplemental training and a new specific/practical exam.

faq.q: What acceptance criteria will I use on D1.1 work?
faq.a: The criteria the contract invokes — D1.1's provisions for the applicable connection type and loading, sometimes modified by owner specifications. Part of Level II competence is confirming the governing edition and any contract amendments before examining, rather than applying remembered limits from prior jobs.

faq.q: How is MT Level 2 different under CP-189 or NAS 410?
faq.a: The role is the same; the rigor is fixed rather than recommended. CP-189 imposes mandatory minimums and requires an ASNT-certified Level III to oversee the program; NAS 410 governs aerospace and adds its own hour and recertification structure. Aerospace and defense contracts commonly specify one of these instead of SNT-TC-1A.

faq.q: How often do I recertify and what does it involve?
faq.a: On the interval your written practice sets — three years is common for Level II, five for Level III — plus annual vision exams. Recertification typically means re-examination or documented continuing satisfactory performance per the written practice; a long break from the method can trigger full re-examination.

title: PT Level 1 Training: 4 Classroom Hours, 70 Hours OJT (SNT-TC-1A)
description: PT Level I needs just 4 classroom hours under SNT-TC-1A — the fastest NDT start. Exams, dwell and rinse skills, vision rules, and which US employers hire first.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Level I: The Quickest Entry Point Into Certified NDT
answer: PT Level I is the fastest NDT certification to reach: SNT-TC-1A recommends just 4 hours of formal classroom training, with 70 hours of PT work experience and 130 total NDT hours. You pass employer-administered general, specific, and practical exams plus annual near-vision and color-differentiation tests. The employer issues the certification. Level I performs the penetrant process under supervision; interpretation belongs to Level II.
expansion: Four classroom hours is the lowest formal-training figure anywhere in the SNT-TC-1A table, and it reflects the method honestly: penetrant testing has little theory but demands absolute process discipline. Capillary action does the physics for you — what the Level I must master is execution: pre-cleaning that actually opens discontinuities, penetrant application and timed dwell, removal that clears background without washing penetrant out of flaws, correct developer application, and honest recording. Over-washing is the classic Level I failure, and it produces the most dangerous outcome in NDT — a clean-looking part with an undetected crack. The experience hours, not the classroom, build that discipline. Most US employers certify PT Level I alongside MT Level I in a single training window because the methods share job sites and the combined class time stays under three days. Full hour tables for every method are at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method.
source: SNT-TC-1A (2024 ed.) recommended training and experience table; ASTM E165; ASME BPVC Section V, Article 6

facets.q: How many hours of training does PT Level 1 require?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A recommends 4 hours of formal classroom training — the lowest of any method — plus 70 hours of PT work experience and 130 total NDT hours. The classroom is typically completed in a single day; the experience hours are the real timeline.

facets.q: Is PT Level 1 the easiest NDT certification to get?
facets.a: It has the smallest classroom requirement, and the process is procedurally simple. But the exams still follow the full three-part structure with 70/80 grading, and the practical demands disciplined execution — over-washing or short dwell times fail candidates who treated it as easy.

facets.q: What can a PT Level 1 do on the job?
facets.a: Perform the penetrant process per written instructions — pre-clean, apply penetrant, time the dwell, remove, develop, and record results — under Level II or III supervision. Interpretation and accept/reject decisions require Level II.

facets.q: Does PT Level 1 require a color vision test?
facets.a: Yes — a color/shade differentiation test plus an annual near-vision exam (Jaeger 2 or equivalent at 12 inches or more). PT depends entirely on seeing red indications against white developer or green fluorescence under UV-A, so color deficiency is a genuine barrier.

facets.q: Should I get PT and MT Level 1 together?
facets.a: Almost always yes. Combined classroom time is only 16 hours, the methods share job sites, and US employers hire surface techs certified in both. Experience hours in each method also count toward the other's total-NDT-hours requirement.

facets.q: What temperature limits apply in penetrant testing?
facets.a: The standard technique window in ASME Section V is 40°F to 125°F for the part and penetrant. Outside that range, the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature using a quench-cracked comparator block — a Level III-controlled process, but Level Is must know the window exists.

sections.heading: Why PT is where most US NDT careers start
paragraphs: Liquid penetrant testing finds surface-breaking discontinuities in any nonporous material — steel, aluminum, titanium, nickel alloys, some plastics and ceramics — using capillary action: penetrant enters the flaw, excess is removed, and a developer draws the trapped penetrant back out into a visible indication. Because the physics is passive, PT training concentrates almost entirely on process execution, and SNT-TC-1A prices that honestly at 4 classroom hours for Level I.

That makes PT the lowest-cost, lowest-risk first certification for both the candidate and the employer. A trainee can complete the classroom in a day, begin logging supervised hours immediately, and be exam-ready within weeks in a busy shop. Employers use PT Level I as the proving ground: a trainee who executes dwell times, wash technique, and documentation with discipline gets invested in for MT, VT, and eventually UT.

Do not mistake low hours for low stakes. PT is trusted for critical work — aerospace fluorescent penetrant inspection of engine components, weld examination on pressure equipment — and a badly washed part passes inspection while carrying a crack. The method is easy to perform and easy to perform wrong, which is exactly why the supervised experience hours exist.

sections.heading: The numbers: 4 classroom hours, 70 method hours, 130 total
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A's recommended initial qualification for PT Level I: 4 hours of formal training, 70 hours of work experience in PT, and 130 hours of total NDT experience. Time in other methods counts toward the 130, so a trainee splitting weeks between PT and MT work accumulates both methods' totals concurrently — the standard pattern in US shops.

The employer's written practice turns these recommendations into binding requirements and may raise them; many aerospace-adjacent employers do. Training-hour reductions for relevant post-secondary education are permitted by SNT-TC-1A's footnotes at the employer's discretion. Candidates skipping Level I and certifying directly to Level II need the cumulative figures: 12 classroom hours, 210 PT hours, 400 total NDT hours.

For the complete per-method, per-level table — including why UT demands ten times PT's classroom hours — see /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method. The national method page at /liquid-penetrant-testing-training covers PT beyond the Level I scope, and /ndt-level-2-training maps the level structure across methods.

sections.heading: The six process steps a Level I must own
paragraphs: Pre-cleaning comes first and fails silently: oil, paint, scale, or machining smear over a flaw's opening and the penetrant never enters. The Level I learns which cleaning methods suit which contamination, and why blasting can peen a crack shut on soft materials. Then penetrant application — spray, brush, or immersion — and dwell time: the procedure-specified minutes the penetrant needs to migrate into discontinuities, tracked honestly, with the clock restarted if penetrant dries.

Removal is where Level Is are made or broken. Solvent-removable technique means wiping — never flooding the surface with solvent, which flushes penetrant straight out of flaws. Water-washable technique means controlled rinsing, with code limits on water temperature and pressure, stopping the moment background clears. Over-removal is invisible: the part looks perfectly clean precisely because you destroyed the evidence.

Developer application and development time complete the process — a thin, even film that draws penetrant back out and spreads it into a readable indication — followed by recording under the required lighting. The Level I documents what appears and calls the Level II; classification and disposition are the next level's job.

sections.heading: The three exams and what the practical actually tests
paragraphs: PT Level I qualification uses SNT-TC-1A's standard exam structure. The general exam covers method fundamentals: capillary action, penetrant types and removal methods, developer forms, contamination effects, and temperature limits. The specific exam covers your employer's procedures, materials, and the specifications its contracts invoke. Both are written; grading requires 70% minimum on each exam and an 80% composite across all three.

The practical is a supervised, graded execution of the full process on test samples containing known discontinuities — typically cracked chrome panels or flawed weld coupons. The Level III's checklist scores each step: cleaning adequacy, dwell timing, removal technique, developer film quality, and whether the known flaws actually produced indications. A candidate who rushes the wash and blanks a known crack fails regardless of written scores.

This is why credible PT Level I training is hands-on despite the 4-hour classroom figure. The lecture content fits in a morning; the afternoon belongs on panels and coupons, building the wash discipline the practical exam — and every job after it — will test.

sections.heading: Vision: the method where the color test earns its keep
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A requires an annual near-vision exam — Jaeger 2 or equivalent at not less than 12 inches, corrective lenses permitted — and a color/shade differentiation test for all certificate holders. In penetrant testing the color requirement is not ceremonial: Type II visible PT is literally the discrimination of red indications against a white developer background, and Type I fluorescent PT is green-yellow emission against violet-dark background under UV-A.

A red-green color deficiency — the most common form, affecting a meaningful fraction of male candidates — directly degrades visible-dye interpretation, and written practices treat a failed differentiation test as disqualifying for the affected techniques. Some employers can accommodate by certifying fluorescent-only scope, where the discrimination is brightness-based; that is a written-practice decision, not a given.

Take the vision tests before booking training. Any occupational health clinic administers Jaeger and color-plate testing in minutes, and confirming your eligibility first protects both your money and your employer's training investment.

sections.heading: What you train on: field kits versus processing lines
paragraphs: US penetrant work splits into two worlds. Field and weld-shop PT runs on portable solvent-removable visible kits — cleaner, red dye penetrant, and nonaqueous developer in aerosols — used on welds, castings, and machined surfaces at ambient conditions. This is where most Level Is start: the technique is Type II visible, Method C solvent-removable, and the skill is wipe-removal discipline and even developer films.

The other world is stationary fluorescent processing — immersion tanks, wash stations, dryers, and developer chambers running Type I fluorescent penetrant on aerospace and high-volume precision components, examined in darkened booths under UV-A lamps meeting minimum intensity requirements. Level Is on these lines learn bath control basics, timed station-to-station processing, and handling that keeps parts uncontaminated between stations.

Training also fixes the boundary conditions in memory: the 40°F-to-125°F standard temperature window, why penetrant families and developers must not be intermixed across manufacturers, and sulfur/halogen contamination limits when testing nickel alloys, titanium, and austenitic stainless — constraints a Level I executes even though a Level III owns the procedure behind them.

sections.heading: Who hires PT Level I techs in the US
paragraphs: Aerospace is the deepest pool: engine overhaul shops, airframe MROs, and precision manufacturers run continuous fluorescent penetrant lines with dedicated processing staff, and FPI processor is a genuine entry job in aviation hubs. Weld fabrication is the second pool — PT covers the stainless and aluminum work MT cannot touch, so shops welding nonmagnetic materials keep PT-certified techs on the floor.

Inspection service companies hire trainees into mixed surface-method roles, dispatching PT alongside MT on piping, vessels, and structural contracts. Foundries and machine shops use PT for in-process checks on castings and finished surfaces. In nearly all these settings the realistic job title is 'NDT trainee' or 'technician' with PT Level I as one line on a growing certification list.

Level I is a wage rung, not a plateau: pay steps up meaningfully at Level II with sign-off authority, and again as methods stack. Current US pay bands by method and level are maintained at /blog/ndt-salary-guide-2026-global — and PT-only careers are rare; treat this certification as the first move in a multi-method sequence.

sections.heading: Getting certified — and how Atlantis runs PT Level I
paragraphs: The sequence: complete documented PT Level I training meeting the 4-hour recommendation, log 70 PT hours and 130 total NDT hours under supervision, pass the general, specific, and practical exams administered under your employer's written practice, pass the vision exams, and receive your employer-issued certification. Employers without a written practice or an in-house Level III can engage Atlantis's outsourced ASNT Level III consulting to stand up the entire program.

Atlantis PT Level I training is deliberately practice-heavy: the theory hours per SNT-TC-1A, then supervised repetitions on cracked panels and weld coupons until wash discipline and developer technique hold up under exam conditions. We bundle PT with MT and VT Level I so one engagement produces a certifiable surface-method tech, delivered at your site or ours. Affordable, accessible, fully customizable — request a quote scoped to your written practice.

Continue with /pt-level-2-training for the interpretation authority this leads to, /liquid-penetrant-testing-training for full method coverage, /ndt-level-2-training for the level framework, and /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method for every method's numbers side by side.

faq.q: Can PT Level 1 classroom training be done in one day?
faq.a: Yes — 4 recommended hours fits comfortably in a single session, and most providers pair it with hands-on panel work the same day. Quality programs still spread practical repetitions across additional sessions, because the practical exam tests execution discipline no lecture provides.

faq.q: Do PT experience hours count toward MT certification?
faq.a: PT hours count toward MT's total NDT experience requirement (130 hours for Level I), but not toward MT's method-specific 70 hours, which must be earned doing magnetic particle work. Running both methods concurrently is the efficient path US shops actually use.

faq.q: What is the difference between visible and fluorescent PT for a Level 1?
faq.a: Visible (Type II) uses red dye read under normal white light — the portable field technique. Fluorescent (Type I) uses UV-A-excited penetrant read in a darkened area and offers higher sensitivity — the stationary aerospace technique. Level I duties are the same process steps; the removal method, lighting, and reading environment differ.

faq.q: How much does PT Level 1 certification cost?
faq.a: There is no ASNT fee — certification is employer-issued under SNT-TC-1A. The costs are tuition, examiner time, consumables, and vision exams. Atlantis quotes PT Level I training on request, typically bundled with MT and VT Level I for a complete surface-method package.

faq.q: Can I certify PT Level 1 with no prior NDT experience?
faq.a: Yes — it is the standard zero-experience entry point. You complete training first, then accumulate the 70 PT hours and 130 total hours as a supervised trainee before sitting the exams. Many employers hire specifically to run candidates through this pipeline.

title: PT Level 2 Training: Hours, ASME V Article 6 Process Combinations
description: PT Level II under SNT-TC-1A: 8 more classroom hours, 140 method hours, and accept/reject authority across ASME Section V Article 6 penetrant process combinations.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Level II: Owning the Process Combinations, Not Just the Process
answer: PT Level II requires 8 additional classroom hours beyond Level I (12 cumulative) and 140 more hours of PT experience (210 cumulative, 400 total NDT hours) under SNT-TC-1A. Level II adds interpretation, accept/reject authority, report sign-off, and supervision — and on ASME code work, command of Section V Article 6's process combinations: penetrant Type, removal Method, and developer form matched correctly to the part and procedure.
expansion: What separates a PT Level II from a competent Level I is not better wiping technique — it is understanding the method as a system of choices. ASME Section V Article 6 structures penetrant testing as combinations: Type I fluorescent or Type II visible penetrant; removal Method A (water-washable), B (lipophilic post-emulsifiable), C (solvent-removable), or D (hydrophilic post-emulsifiable); and developer forms from dry powder to water-soluble, water-suspendible, and nonaqueous. Each combination carries its own sensitivities, failure modes, and procedural controls, and the Level II must execute whichever combination the qualified procedure invokes, recognize when process conditions have drifted outside it, and interpret what the resulting indications mean. The Level II also owns the numbers: the 40°F-125°F standard temperature window, UV-A intensity minimums, and rinse-water limits. Cumulative hour tables for every method are at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method.
source: SNT-TC-1A (2024 ed.) recommended training and experience table; ASME BPVC Section V, Article 6; ASTM E165
