Standard technique temperature window: 40°F–125°F; outside it, the procedure is qualified with a quench-cracked comparator block.

facets.q: How many hours do I need for PT Level 2?
facets.a: Beyond Level I: 8 more classroom hours and 140 more hours of PT experience. Cumulative from zero: 12 classroom hours, 210 hours in PT, and 400 total NDT hours. Direct-to-Level-II candidates must present the cumulative totals.

facets.q: What are the ASME Section V Article 6 process combinations?
facets.a: Penetrant Type (I fluorescent, II visible) combined with removal Method (A water-washable, B lipophilic post-emulsifiable, C solvent-removable, D hydrophilic post-emulsifiable) and a developer form — dry, water-soluble, water-suspendible, or nonaqueous. The qualified procedure fixes the combination; the Level II executes and polices it.

facets.q: What temperature range is allowed for penetrant testing?
facets.a: The standard technique covers part and penetrant temperatures of 40°F to 125°F. Outside that window, ASME Section V requires qualifying the procedure at the actual temperature by demonstration on a quench-cracked comparator block — a Level III-governed qualification the Level II must know to demand.

facets.q: What UV light intensity does fluorescent PT require?
facets.a: A minimum of 1000 µW/cm² UV-A at the examination surface, verified with a calibrated radiometer, in an examination area darkened to a low ambient white-light level. Checking and logging lamp intensity is a Level II responsibility that audits routinely target.

facets.q: Can a PT Level 2 write procedures?
facets.a: No — procedure approval is Level III territory. A Level II works to qualified procedures, may prepare written instructions for Level Is under many written practices, interprets results, and signs reports. Confusing these boundaries is a recurring audit finding.

facets.q: What does the PT Level 2 practical exam involve?
facets.a: Full examinations on flawed samples using the employer's techniques: process execution, indication classification as relevant, non-relevant, or false, disposition against stated acceptance criteria, and a signed report. Grading is checklist-based by a Level III, with the 70/80 SNT-TC-1A rule applied across all three exams.

sections.heading: Level II authority: interpretation, disposition, signature
paragraphs: PT Level II is the first level authorized to run a penetrant examination end-to-end alone: set up per the qualified procedure, execute the process, interpret every indication, evaluate relevant ones against the governing acceptance criteria, accept or reject, and sign the report. Level II also supervises — a single Level II legitimizes the process work of multiple Level Is, which is how FPI lines and field crews actually staff.

The interpretation burden in PT is subtler than newcomers expect. Bleed-out behavior carries information: a crack re-bleeds after wipe-off and grows as a sharp continuous line; porosity presents as rounded, discrete indications; lint, poor wash, and developer damage produce false indications a Level II must recognize and re-process rather than report. Time-based observation — watching how fast and how large an indication develops — is a genuine diagnostic skill.

Then evaluation: acceptance criteria come from the referencing code section — ASME Section VIII, B31.3, or the contract's invoked standard — not from Article 6 itself, which governs how to examine, not what to accept. Knowing which document supplies the criteria on each job is baseline Level II competence.

sections.heading: The numbers: +8 classroom hours, +140 method hours
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A recommends 8 additional formal training hours for PT Level II on top of Level I's 4 — 12 cumulative — plus 140 additional hours of PT experience beyond Level I's 70, for 210 cumulative in-method within 400 total NDT hours. A candidate certifying directly to Level II presents the cumulative figures in full.

Notice the structure: PT Level II classroom hours double the method's Level I figure, the reverse of MT's front-loaded pattern. The committee's logic is that PT's execution basics are quick to teach, but the Level II layer — process combinations, control checks, interpretation, code interfaces — is where the real instructional content lives. Your employer's written practice remains the binding document and may exceed these recommendations, particularly in aerospace-adjacent shops.

The complete per-method, per-level hour tables are consolidated at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method. The method overview lives at /liquid-penetrant-testing-training, this certification's prerequisite at /pt-level-1-training, and the cross-method level framework at /ndt-level-2-training.

sections.heading: Article 6 as a decision system: Type × Method × developer
paragraphs: ASME Section V Article 6 organizes penetrant testing into combinable elements. Penetrant Type: I fluorescent, read under UV-A in a darkened area, higher sensitivity; II visible, red dye read under adequate white light, field-portable. Removal Method: A water-washable, B lipophilic post-emulsifiable, C solvent-removable, D hydrophilic post-emulsifiable. Developer form: dry powder, water-soluble, water-suspendible, or nonaqueous — each with its own application rules and reading characteristics.

The qualified procedure fixes the combination for a given examination; the Level II's job is to execute it exactly and to recognize what each element demands. Method A tolerates rough surfaces but over-washes easily. Method B's lipophilic emulsifier works on contact time — seconds matter. Method C lives and dies on wipe discipline. Method D, the aerospace-line standard, turns removal into a controlled chemical process with concentration verification.

Interchanging elements is not permitted casually: penetrant families, emulsifiers, and developers are qualified together, and mixing manufacturers or substituting a developer form can invalidate the examination. A Level II who catches an unqualified substitution before parts run is doing precisely the job the certification exists for.

sections.heading: The numbers Article 6 makes you own: temperature, light, water
paragraphs: The standard technique applies between 40°F and 125°F — part surface and penetrant both. Below 40°F, penetrant viscosity and water behavior degrade capillary entry; above 125°F, penetrant dries in the flaw. Work outside the window requires qualifying the procedure at the actual temperature by comparative demonstration on a quench-cracked block, one half processed at standard temperature, one at the proposed condition. Level IIs on outdoor winter jobs must know this rule cold, because schedule pressure will test it.

Fluorescent examination requires a minimum of 1000 µW/cm² UV-A intensity at the examination surface, verified with a calibrated radiometer, in an area darkened to a low ambient white-light level; visible examination requires adequate white light at the surface, commonly specified at 100 footcandles. Lamp warm-up, intensity logging, and light-meter calibration status are Level II checklist items, and they are among the most-cited findings in PT audits.

Water-washable and post-emulsifiable rinsing carries its own limits — commonly a maximum of 110°F water temperature and 50 psi spray pressure — because hot, high-pressure water strips penetrant from flaws exactly as effectively as it clears background. The Level II enforces these numbers against the strong human tendency to rinse harder when background is stubborn.

sections.heading: Where Level IIs earn their pay: removal control and process drift
paragraphs: Over-removal remains the method's cardinal sin at every level, but the Level II must detect it systemically, not just avoid it personally. Signs of process drift: fluorescent background dimming shift over shift as emulsifier concentration creeps, wash stations running hotter than logged, developer films going from translucent to chalky. A Level II reading only indications, and never the process, will eventually pass a cracked part.

Control checks are the countermeasure. Known-defect comparator panels run through the line verify the system still finds what it must find; emulsifier concentration checks, penetrant contamination checks, and UV intensity logs each guard a specific failure mode. Under most written practices the Level II performs and records these; the Level III sets their frequency and acts on adverse trends.

Interpretation under drift is the advanced skill: distinguishing a weak indication caused by a tight flaw from one caused by degraded process sensitivity. The honest answer is often re-cleaning and re-processing the part — a call that costs an hour and saves a failure investigation.

sections.heading: The Level II exams: what changes from Level I
paragraphs: The general exam moves from process recall to method command: selecting combinations for described scenarios, sensitivity rankings across Types and Methods, temperature and lighting requirements, contamination restrictions for titanium and nickel alloys, and the method's hard limits — PT finds only surface-breaking discontinuities, full stop. Expect questions that give you a part, a material, and a condition, and require the defensible technique.

The specific exam tests your employer's qualified procedures and the codes its contracts invoke — for ASME shops, Article 6 requirements and the referencing code's acceptance criteria. The practical requires complete examinations on flawed samples: correct execution, every indication classified, relevant indications dispositioned against stated criteria, and a report written and signed as a customer would receive it. The 70% per-exam, 80% composite rule applies.

Recertification follows your written practice's interval — commonly three years — with annual vision exams including color differentiation throughout. Method continuity matters: extended interruption from PT work can trigger re-examination, so keep experience logs current.

sections.heading: US demand and pay for PT Level II
paragraphs: Aerospace carries the deepest structural demand: FPI lines at engine overhaul shops and airframe MROs run under stringent process control and need Level IIs to read parts and police the line. ASME fabrication — pressure vessels, process piping — needs PT Level IIs for stainless and nonferrous welds where MT cannot go. Inspection service companies dispatch PT II as part of the standard surface-method bundle on refinery, chemical-plant, and pipeline work.

PT Level II rarely appears alone in postings; MT II + PT II is the US surface-tech standard, with VT II increasingly attached. Compensation sits in the same band as MT Level II — above trainee rates, below UT — and climbs with method stacking and code fluency. An FPI Level II with hydrophilic-line process-control experience commands a premium in aviation markets. Current US bands by method, level, and sector: /blog/ndt-salary-guide-2026-global.

For employers, an in-house PT Level II converts recurring subcontract spend on stainless weld examination into same-day internal capability — usually the shortest payback of any NDT training investment because the equipment cost is trivial.

sections.heading: Getting there with Atlantis
paragraphs: Atlantis PT Level II training is built around Article 6's decision structure: classroom hours per SNT-TC-1A covering all four removal methods and developer forms, control-check practice, and interpretation work on flawed samples spanning weld, casting, and machined-surface indications. Exam banks and practical checklists are provided for your Level III — or our outsourced ASNT Level III consulting administers qualification end-to-end, written practice included.

We deliver at your facility or ours, and most employers pair PT Level II with MT Level II in one engagement to complete a surface-method bench. Affordable, accessible, fully customizable — request a quote and we will scope the program to your procedures, your product forms, and the codes your contracts invoke.

Related pages: /pt-level-1-training for the prerequisite, /liquid-penetrant-testing-training for the method overview, /ndt-level-2-training for how Level II works across methods, and /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method for the full hour tables.

faq.q: Can I certify PT Level 2 directly without Level 1?
faq.a: Yes. SNT-TC-1A allows direct Level II certification against the cumulative requirements — 12 classroom hours, 210 PT hours, 400 total NDT hours — plus the Level II exams. It is the normal route for experienced techs changing employers, since certification does not transfer but documented hours do.

faq.q: Does PT Level 2 under SNT-TC-1A satisfy ASME Code work?
faq.a: Yes — ASME Section V requires NDE personnel qualified per the employer's written practice based on SNT-TC-1A (or CP-189), and the referencing code sections invoke that framework. Your employer's written practice and your documented qualification records are what an Authorized Inspector examines.

faq.q: What is the difference between Method B and Method D emulsifiers?
faq.a: Method B uses a lipophilic (oil-based) emulsifier applied undiluted by immersion, acting fast on contact. Method D uses a hydrophilic (water-dilutable, detergent-type) emulsifier with a pre-rinse and controlled concentration, giving finer removal control. Method D dominates modern aerospace FPI lines precisely because its variables are measurable and enforceable.

faq.q: Why can't I use any developer with any penetrant?
faq.a: Penetrant, emulsifier, and developer are qualified as a family; sensitivities and chemical compatibilities are demonstrated for the combination, not the components. Substituting across manufacturers or swapping developer forms outside the qualified procedure can suppress indications and invalidates the examination under Article 6.

faq.q: How long does Level I to PT Level 2 progression take?
faq.a: The 140 additional method hours amount to roughly one to three months of PT-heavy full-time work, longer where PT is intermittent. The 8 classroom hours typically run mid-progression so exams follow immediately once hours complete — a cadence Atlantis schedules routinely for client shops.

title: VT Level 1 Training: 8 Hours Class, 70 Hours OJT (SNT-TC-1A)
description: VT Level I under SNT-TC-1A: 8 classroom hours and 70 method hours. Direct vs remote visual, lighting minimums, vision tests, and what Level I may sign on the job.
h1: Visual Testing Level I: The Method Every Other Method Depends On
answer: VT Level I under SNT-TC-1A requires 8 hours of formal classroom training, 70 hours of visual testing experience, and 130 total NDT hours, followed by employer-administered general, specific, and practical exams. Annual near-vision (Jaeger 2 or equivalent at 12 inches minimum) and color-differentiation tests apply. Level I performs direct visual examinations per written instructions and records results; interpretation and acceptance belong to Level II.
expansion: Visual testing is the first examination every code requires and the one every other NDT method silently depends on — a surface not visually examined and prepared correctly compromises the MT, PT, or UT that follows. Yet VT is the method most often performed by people with no formal qualification at all, which is exactly why contracts increasingly demand certified personnel. The Level I's scope is disciplined observation: direct visual examination within defined eye-to-surface distance and viewing angle, under verified lighting, using measuring tools per a written instruction, with honest recording. ASME Section V Article 9 defines direct visual examination as the eye within 24 inches of the surface at an angle not less than 30 degrees — geometry a Level I applies physically on every access decision. The 8 classroom hours cover more measurement technique than any other method's entry course. Full hour tables: /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method.

facets.q: How many training hours does VT Level 1 require?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A recommends 8 hours of formal training, 70 hours of VT work experience, and 130 total NDT hours. The classroom fits in one to two days; the experience hours accumulate quickly because visual examination is continuous on fabrication work.

facets.q: What is direct visual examination under ASME Section V?
facets.a: Examination with the eye within 24 inches of the surface at a viewing angle of at least 30 degrees, under verified adequate lighting. When that geometry cannot be achieved, mirrors extend access or the examination becomes remote — borescopes, cameras — with resolution requirements of its own.

facets.q: Can a VT Level 1 accept welds?
facets.a: No. Level I examines per written instructions, measures, and records. Comparing findings against acceptance criteria and making the accept/reject call requires Level II. Contracts specifying certified visual examination mean Level II signatures.

facets.q: What lighting is required for visual testing?
facets.a: Adequate illumination at the examination surface verified with a light meter — 100 footcandles is the commonly invoked code minimum for examination. Level Is verify and log the light level; an examination performed under unverified or inadequate light is an invalid examination.

facets.q: Is VT Level 1 worth getting on its own?
facets.a: As a standalone, rarely — its value is as the third leg of the MT/PT/VT surface package, adding one to two classroom days to a training window employers are already funding. It is also the natural first rung toward VT Level II, which contracts actually name.

facets.q: What vision requirements apply to VT?
facets.a: Annual near-vision acuity of Jaeger 2 or equivalent at not less than 12 inches, corrected vision permitted, plus color/shade differentiation. Some customer specifications tighten acuity to Jaeger 1 for visual examiners — check the contract, not just the written practice.

sections.heading: The method hiding in plain sight
paragraphs: Every weld ever accepted was examined visually first. Codes sequence it that way deliberately: visual examination catches undercut, underfill, surface porosity, overlap, and misalignment before more expensive methods run, and a surface that fails visual is repaired before MT, PT, or UT is wasted on it. Visual testing is the highest-volume examination in industry — and historically the least formally qualified, performed by whoever was standing nearest the weld.

That informality is disappearing. ASME Section V Article 9 defines visual examination requirements, referencing codes require documented examiner qualification, and customer contracts increasingly write 'personnel certified to SNT-TC-1A VT Level II' into quality clauses. The result is real demand for a certification that costs less classroom time than almost anything else in NDT.

VT Level I is where that qualification starts: disciplined, documented observation under a written instruction. It converts 'looking at the weld' into an examination — defined access geometry, verified lighting, calibrated measuring tools, and a record. The distinction sounds bureaucratic until an undercut weld reaches service because nobody with defined responsibility ever formally looked.

sections.heading: The numbers: 8 classroom hours, 70 method hours, 130 total
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A recommends 8 hours of formal training for VT Level I — double PT's figure, two-thirds of MT's — plus 70 hours of VT experience and 130 total NDT hours. The classroom weighting reflects content: VT training is dense with measurement technique, tooling, and access rules rather than physics. Experience accumulates fast because fabrication work generates continuous visual examination opportunity in a way bench MT or PT batches do not.

The employer's written practice makes these numbers binding and may raise them; education-based training-hour reductions are permitted at employer discretion per SNT-TC-1A's footnotes. Direct certification to Level II requires the cumulative totals — 24 classroom hours, 210 VT hours, 400 total NDT hours — with nothing waived.

Cross-method hour tables are consolidated at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method. For the method beyond Level I scope see /visual-testing-training, and for how Level I functions across all methods see /ndt-level-1-training. The certification this one feeds — the one contracts actually name — is at /vt-level-2-training.

sections.heading: Direct versus remote visual: the 24-inch, 30-degree rule
paragraphs: ASME Section V Article 9 defines direct visual examination by geometry: the eye within 24 inches of the examination surface, at a viewing angle not less than 30 degrees to that surface. This is not trivia — it is a physical access standard a Level I applies constantly. A weld root visible only at a grazing 15-degree angle from 30 inches away has not been visually examined, whatever the technician believes they saw.

Mirrors extend direct examination into bores, behind flanges, and around corners while preserving the geometry requirements. When access defeats direct examination entirely, the examination becomes remote — borescopes, fiberscopes, cameras — and remote systems must demonstrate resolution at least equivalent to direct viewing, typically via a resolution test target. Remote VT is generally a Level II-and-above technique decision, but Level Is work as the second set of hands on it.

Level I training drills the access decision: can this surface be examined directly, what aid restores compliant geometry, and when must the instruction's technique be escalated rather than improvised? Honest escalation — 'I cannot see this properly' — is a certifiable skill, and the practical exam probes for it.

sections.heading: Lighting: the 100-footcandle discipline
paragraphs: Visual examination requires verified adequate illumination at the surface — 100 footcandles is the commonly invoked minimum for examination under ASME-referencing work. The operative word is verified: a Level I carries a calibrated light meter, measures at the examination surface, and logs the reading. Shop lighting that feels bright routinely measures below threshold inside nozzles, under vessel skirts, and on night-shift field work.

The failure mode is silent, like PT over-washing: an examination under inadequate light looks identical to a valid one on paper unless the light reading was never taken or never honest. Auditors know this, which is why light-meter calibration stickers and logged readings are among the first records requested in VT audits.

Training covers supplemental lighting technique as well — flashlight angle for revealing surface relief, raking light to make undercut and shallow porosity cast shadows, avoiding glare washout on shiny machined surfaces. Lighting is the VT equivalent of magnetization direction in MT: the variable that determines whether a real flaw is visible at all.

sections.heading: Tools of the trade: gauges, mirrors, and the measuring discipline
paragraphs: VT is the most tool-intensive entry-level method. The bridge cam gauge measures weld reinforcement, undercut depth, fillet size, and misalignment; fillet gauge sets check leg length and concavity; V-WAC and pit gauges quantify undercut and corrosion depth; taper gauges size gaps. Level I training puts hours into reading these correctly, because a measurement error translates directly into a wrong disposition by the Level II relying on the recorded data.

Inspection mirrors, magnifiers up to the powers the procedure permits, flashlights, and surface-temperature-safe marking materials round out the kit. Traceability matters even here: measuring tools carry calibration status, and using an out-of-calibration gauge invalidates the measurements it produced — a detail written practices and auditors both enforce.

The recording discipline is the other half of the toolkit: location referencing on the part, indication dimensions, and unambiguous description in the terminology of the governing code — undercut, not 'groove'; incomplete fusion, not 'bad spot'. Level Is who record in code language make their Level IIs faster and their employers audit-proof.

sections.heading: Vision requirements: nowhere are they more literal
paragraphs: Every SNT-TC-1A certificate holder takes an annual near-vision exam — Jaeger 2 or equivalent at not less than 12 inches, corrected vision acceptable — plus color and shade differentiation. In VT the connection between the test and the job is one-to-one: the certified instrument is the examiner's eye. Some customer specifications and codes tighten the acuity requirement for visual examiners to Jaeger 1; the contract governs, so check it rather than assuming the written-practice default.

Shade differentiation matters more than pure color in much VT work — distinguishing heat tint gradations on stainless, oxide films, and the subtle contrast between a tight crack and a scratch on as-welded surfaces. The color test also protects downstream method work, since VT-certified techs typically hold MT and PT as well.

As with the other surface methods: test your vision before funding training. Annual re-tests are a compliance item forever after — an expired vision exam suspends the certification it supports, and suspended certs discovered mid-audit unwind every examination signed since expiry.

sections.heading: The exams, and who hires VT Level I in the US
paragraphs: Qualification follows the standard three-exam structure: a general exam on visual fundamentals — optics basics, lighting, access geometry, discontinuity types by process; a specific exam on your employer's instructions and governing codes; and a practical exam examining and measuring real weld samples, graded by checklist, with results recorded correctly. The 70% per-exam, 80% composite rule applies. For Level I, the practical emphasizes measurement accuracy and honest recording over disposition, which is reserved for Level II.

Hiring reality: VT Level I is almost never a standalone job. It is the third certification on a surface-method trainee's card — MT, PT, VT in one training window — and the qualification that lets a fabrication shop's QC department put trainees on documented weld checks legitimately. Steel fabricators, pipe shops, vessel manufacturers, and inspection service companies all consume it this way.

The pay story is the surface-tech story: Level I is the trainee band, and the step-change arrives at Level II with signature authority — see /blog/ndt-salary-guide-2026-global for current US bands. VT's particular leverage is upward: VT Level II is the certification contracts name, and it shares DNA with CWI and API inspection credentials that define the profession's upper rungs.

sections.heading: Getting certified — and how Atlantis runs VT Level I
paragraphs: The path: 8 documented classroom hours, 70 VT hours and 130 total NDT hours under supervision, three exams administered under your employer's written practice, annual vision exams, employer-issued certification. No written practice or Level III in-house? Atlantis's outsourced ASNT Level III consulting supplies both — written practice authorship, exam administration, and certification records built to survive audit.

Atlantis VT Level I training is measurement-heavy by design: gauge work on real weld samples, light-meter discipline, access-geometry drills, and recording practice in code terminology. It slots into the same engagement as MT and PT Level I, producing a fully certified surface-method trainee in a single training window at your site or ours. Affordable, accessible, fully customizable — request a quote scoped to your written practice.

Where to go next: /vt-level-2-training for the certification contracts actually specify, /visual-testing-training for full method coverage, /ndt-level-1-training for the level framework, and /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method for every method's hours in one table.

faq.q: Is VT Level 1 required before welding inspection jobs?
faq.a: It is the fastest legitimate credential for documented weld checks, but note the distinction: AWS D1.1 structural visual inspection is the CWI's domain, while ASME and API-world contracts reference SNT-TC-1A VT. VT Level I starts the SNT-TC-1A track; inspection sign-off in either world requires the next level up.

faq.q: Can welders count their experience toward VT hours?
faq.a: Welding itself does not count, but documented time performing visual examination of welds under a certified Level II or III does — and welders transitioning into QC accumulate those hours quickly. The 130 total NDT hours can include MT and PT time logged in the same period.

faq.q: Does VT Level 1 cover borescope inspection?
faq.a: Level I training introduces remote visual concepts, but borescope examinations are typically run under Level II technique decisions, with resolution verification requirements. Deep remote-VT work — tubes, turbines, internals — is usually a Level II scope with equipment-specific training on top.

faq.q: How long does the whole VT Level 1 process take?
faq.a: Classroom in one to two days; the 70 method hours in two to four weeks of fabrication-floor work where visual examination is continuous; exams immediately after. Bundled with MT and PT, the complete surface-method Level I package typically runs a few months end to end, driven by experience hours.

faq.q: What does VT Level 1 training cost?
faq.a: There is no ASNT fee — certification is employer-issued. Costs are tuition, examiner time, and vision exams, and VT adds the least incremental cost of any method to an existing MT/PT training engagement. Atlantis quotes on request, bundled or standalone.

title: VT Level 2 Training: Why It's Often the Contractual Minimum
description: VT Level II is the minimum many US contracts accept for weld visual examination. Hours, exam content, ASME and API context, and practice questions to prepare.
h1: Visual Testing Level II: The Most Under-Rated Certification in NDT
answer: VT Level II requires 16 additional classroom hours beyond Level I (24 cumulative) and 140 more hours of VT experience (210 cumulative, 400 total NDT hours) under SNT-TC-1A. It grants what contracts actually demand: authority to examine, evaluate against acceptance criteria, accept or reject, and sign. On ASME, API, and owner-specification work, 'VT Level II per SNT-TC-1A' is routinely the written contractual minimum for visual examination personnel.
expansion: No certification in NDT is more under-rated relative to how often it is contractually required. Quality clauses across pressure-equipment fabrication, piping construction, and in-service inspection name SNT-TC-1A VT Level II as the minimum qualification for personnel performing and dispositioning visual examinations — because every code-governed weld is visually examined and someone qualified must sign that examination. Yet techs chase UT hours while treating VT as a checkbox, and shops discover at contract award that nobody on staff can legally sign the visual reports. The Level II owns acceptance criteria fluency — undercut limits, reinforcement profiles, surface porosity, fill and fusion conditions per the referencing code — plus the technique authority for remote and direct examination. The certification also stacks: it is the natural bridge toward CWI and API 510/570/653 credentials. Test yourself against real exam-style items at /blog/vt-level-2-practice-questions; hour tables for all methods at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method.

facets.q: How many hours do I need for VT Level 2?
facets.a: Beyond Level I: 16 more classroom hours and 140 more VT experience hours. Cumulative from zero: 24 classroom hours, 210 hours in VT, 400 total NDT hours. Note VT Level II's classroom increment is the largest of the surface methods — double MT's.

facets.q: Why do contracts specify VT Level 2 as a minimum?
facets.a: Because every code weld requires visual examination and a qualified signature on it. Naming 'SNT-TC-1A VT Level II' in the quality clause gives buyers an auditable, standard qualification floor. Shops without one on staff cannot self-perform even the visual scope.

facets.q: Is VT Level 2 the same as a CWI?
facets.a: No. The CWI is an AWS central certification covering D1.1-world visual inspection duties; VT Level II is employer-issued under SNT-TC-1A and governs ASME/API-world visual examination. The knowledge overlaps heavily — many techs hold both — but neither substitutes for the other contractually.

facets.q: What acceptance criteria does a VT Level 2 apply?
facets.a: Whatever the referencing code supplies: reinforcement, undercut, porosity, and fusion limits from ASME Section VIII or B31.3 tables, tank criteria under API 653, or owner-spec amendments. Article 9 tells you how to examine; the referencing code tells you what to accept.

facets.q: Where can I practice for the VT Level 2 exam?
facets.a: Work through exam-style questions at /blog/vt-level-2-practice-questions — general-exam items on optics, lighting, and access geometry plus criteria-application questions matching the specific exam's difficulty. Pair it with hands-on gauge work; the practical exam is measured, not memorized.

facets.q: Does VT Level 2 help toward API 510 or 570?
facets.a: Directly. API inspector work leans on visual examination competence, and documented VT Level II experience strengthens both the application and the exam preparation. The VT II → API credential path is one of the highest-return progressions in US inspection careers.

sections.heading: The most under-rated certification in NDT — and why that is an opportunity
paragraphs: Technicians rank certifications by perceived sophistication: UT and phased array at the top, VT somewhere near the bottom. Contracts rank them by what must be signed — and by that measure VT Level II outranks its reputation everywhere. Every code-governed weld gets a visual examination, visual findings gate every subsequent NDE method, and quality clauses across ASME and API work name SNT-TC-1A VT Level II as the minimum qualification for the person signing.

The mismatch creates a standing arbitrage. Shops bid work, win it, and then discover the NDE clause requires a certified visual examiner they do not employ — subcontracting a capability that costs 24 classroom hours to build in-house. Techs skip VT II while grinding UT hours, leaving signature authority on the single highest-volume examination to someone else.

This page covers the certification the market underprices: the hours, the authority, where codes invoke it, what the exams contain, and the one place — AWS D1.1 structural visual — where it does not substitute for a different credential. If you hold VT Level I, this is the level where the certification starts paying.

sections.heading: The numbers: +16 classroom hours, +140 method hours
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A recommends 16 additional formal training hours for VT Level II — the largest Level II classroom increment among the surface methods, double the Level I figure — bringing the cumulative total to 24 hours. Experience: 140 additional VT hours beyond Level I's 70, for 210 cumulative in-method within 400 total NDT hours. Direct-to-Level-II candidates present the cumulative figures.

The heavy classroom weighting is meaningful: Level II VT content is acceptance-criteria fluency across referencing codes, discontinuity metallurgy by welding process, remote visual technique and resolution verification, and evaluation methodology — genuinely instructional material, unlike experience-driven MT interpretation. This is a certification where the coursework does substantial work.

Your employer's written practice sets the binding requirements. Cross-method hour tables are at /blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method; the prerequisite level at /vt-level-1-training; the method overview at /visual-testing-training; the cross-method Level II framework at /ndt-level-2-training.

sections.heading: Where the codes put you: ASME, API — and the D1.1 exception
paragraphs: On ASME work, Article 9 of Section V defines how visual examination is performed — direct examination within 24 inches at not less than 30 degrees, verified lighting, documented technique — while the referencing code supplies acceptance criteria and requires qualified examiners. B31.3 piping construction and Section VIII vessel fabrication both run on this structure, and SNT-TC-1A VT Level II is the standard qualification demonstration. The Level II performs, dispositions, signs, and generates the records that feed code data reports.

In the API in-service world — 510 pressure vessels, 570 piping, 653 tanks — certified API inspectors direct inspection programs but rely on qualified NDE personnel to execute examination scopes. VT Level IIs perform the visual scope of internal inspections, corrosion surveys, and repair acceptance, which is why inspection contractors staff them in quantity around refinery turnaround seasons.

The exception to memorize: AWS D1.1 assigns structural visual inspection duties to AWS Certified Welding Inspectors or engineer-approved equivalents — a VT Level II certificate alone does not satisfy D1.1's visual inspection clause. Shops spanning both worlds staff both credentials, and technicians holding both are disproportionately valuable. Misreading which qualification a contract's visual clause names is a recurring and expensive procurement error.

sections.heading: What the Level II must evaluate: criteria fluency
paragraphs: The core Level II skill is applying acceptance criteria precisely. Undercut is the canonical example: limits vary by referencing code, weld type, and sometimes material thickness — a depth acceptable under one code section is rejectable under another. The Level II measures with a calibrated gauge, identifies the governing criterion for this weld on this contract, and dispositions accordingly. Approximation and memory-of-the-last-job are the two failure patterns.

The evaluation inventory spans reinforcement height and profile, surface porosity size and distribution, incomplete fusion and overlap at visible edges, crater conditions, arc strikes, spatter where prohibited, misalignment, and weld size on fillets. Each carries a measurable limit and a correct gauge. Beyond welds, in-service VT adds corrosion assessment — pitting depth and density, general loss patterns — feeding API inspection evaluations.

Discontinuity metallurgy makes evaluation faster and more defensible: knowing that crater cracks live at stops, that undercut follows excessive travel speed or current, that a given process typically produces given surface conditions. The Level II who understands why a discontinuity forms recognizes it earlier and testifies to it more credibly in dispute.

sections.heading: Exam content — and where to practice
paragraphs: The general exam covers vision and optics fundamentals, illumination requirements and verification, direct and remote examination technique, access geometry, measurement tooling, and discontinuity identification by origin. The specific exam is built from your employer's procedures and the codes on its contracts — expect criteria-application questions: given this indication, this measurement, this code, disposition it. The practical requires examining flawed weld samples, measuring correctly, dispositioning against stated criteria, and producing a signed report. Grading: 70% minimum each exam, 80% composite.

We maintain a bank of exam-style questions at /blog/vt-level-2-practice-questions — general-exam items and criteria-application drills at representative difficulty. Working through it before your exam window is the cheapest available confidence check, and it will locate your gaps faster than re-reading course notes.

A preparation note from exam administration experience: candidates fail the practical on measurement technique more than on knowledge — inconsistent gauge seating, unlogged lighting checks, findings recorded without location reference. Drill the mechanics until they are boring; the knowledge rides on top of them.

sections.heading: Career leverage: the bridge certification
paragraphs: VT Level II sits at the junction of NDT and inspection careers. Toward NDT, it completes the surface-method Level II package with MT and PT, making a technician independently dispatchable on the full non-volumetric scope. Toward inspection, its content — criteria fluency, weld discontinuity evaluation, documentation discipline — is the direct foundation for the AWS CWI and the API 510/570/653 credentials that anchor the profession's highest-paid non-Level-III roles.

That bridging quality shows up in earnings progression. A VT II holder who adds a CWI or an API credential moves from the technician pay structure into the inspector structure — a step-change rather than a raise. Current US bands by certification and sector are maintained at /blog/ndt-salary-guide-2026-global; the pattern to notice is how consistently the inspection-credential rows sit above the single-method technician rows.

For employers the leverage is contractual: one VT Level II on staff converts subcontracted visual scopes into self-performed work and satisfies the quality-clause minimums that gate bid lists. Few certifications buy market access this cheaply — 24 cumulative classroom hours against contract eligibility.

sections.heading: Level II authority in practice: supervising and technique decisions
paragraphs: Level II authority extends past evaluation into technique and supervision. The Level II selects examination aids within the procedure — deciding when mirrors preserve direct-examination geometry, when the job goes remote, and verifying that remote systems resolve to the required standard before use. Lighting strategy, surface preparation adequacy, and examination timing relative to welding (criteria that apply after cooling, delayed examination where specified) are Level II calls.

Supervision is the force multiplier: Level Is and trainees examine and measure under the Level II's direction, and the Level II's review and signature make their output contractually valid. On a turnaround or a fabrication surge, one Level II running four trainees is the difference between self-performing the visual scope and subcontracting it.

The boundary above remains: procedures and written practices are Level III instruments, and technique deviations beyond procedure limits require Level III disposition. Atlantis provides that layer as outsourced ASNT Level III consulting for shops without one in-house — the same engagement that administers Level II qualification.

paragraphs: Atlantis VT Level II training delivers the 16-hour Level II curriculum against SNT-TC-1A topic recommendations: acceptance-criteria application across ASME and API referencing codes, gauge technique on flawed weld samples, remote visual and resolution verification, and report writing that survives customer audit. Exam banks and practical checklists come ready for your Level III — or our outsourced Level III service administers qualification end-to-end, written practice included.

faq.q: Can I certify VT Level 2 directly without holding Level 1?
faq.a: Yes — present the cumulative requirements: 24 classroom hours, 210 VT hours, 400 total NDT hours, then pass the Level II exams under the employer's written practice. Experienced QC personnel and welders moving into examination roles commonly document prior supervised visual hours toward the total.

faq.q: Is VT Level 2 enough to sign visual reports on ASME code jobs?
faq.a: Yes, where the employer's qualification program certifies you and the referencing code's requirements are met — that combination is exactly what B31.3 and Section VIII work expects. The Authorized Inspector will verify your certification records against the written practice, so documentation completeness matters as much as the card.

faq.q: Why doesn't VT Level 2 cover AWS D1.1 visual inspection?
faq.a: D1.1 assigns visual inspection duties to AWS CWIs, CAWIs under supervision, or engineer-approved equivalents — a code-specific personnel rule, not a judgment on VT II competence. Some engineers approve experienced VT Level IIs as equivalents, but that is a project-level decision, never an entitlement. Structural shops staff CWIs for this reason.

faq.q: How long does VT Level 1 to Level 2 take?
faq.a: The 140 additional method hours represent roughly one to three months of examination-heavy work; the 16 classroom hours run in two to three training days scheduled mid-progression. Candidates using /blog/vt-level-2-practice-questions during the experience window typically sit exams immediately when hours complete.

faq.q: Which should I get first — VT Level 2 or my UT hours?
faq.a: If your employer's contracts name visual examiner minimums, VT Level II first: it is 16 classroom hours against immediate signature authority and bid-list eligibility, while UT Level II is a 40-plus-hour classroom and 1,200-total-hour commitment. The certifications are complementary, but VT II pays back on a far shorter cycle.

faq.q: Does VT Level 2 expire?
faq.a: It runs on your written practice's recertification interval — commonly three years — with annual near-vision and periodic color-differentiation exams throughout. An expired vision exam suspends the certification, and examinations signed under a lapsed cert unwind in audit, so calendar the annual exam as rigidly as the recert.

sections.heading: What drives NDT demand in the Pacific Northwest
paragraphs: The Pacific Northwest NDT market is aerospace-led to a degree no other US region matches. Boeing's Everett and Renton assembly plants anchor a supplier base spread through Auburn, Kent, Sumner, and Frederickson in Washington and into the Portland metro in Oregon — machine shops, composite layup facilities, casting and forging plants, and processing houses that all carry NDT requirements flowed down from prime contracts. When a supplier wins aerospace work, the contract flows down NAS 410 certification requirements, and that single fact shapes most of the training demand in the region.

The second tier of demand comes from the water: Puget Sound holds the largest concentration of naval ship maintenance on the US West Coast, with the naval shipyard at Bremerton and commercial yards in Seattle, Tacoma, and Portland pulling weld inspection continuously. The third tier is hydro — the Columbia and Snake River dam system is the largest hydroelectric complex in the United States, and its penstocks, turbine runners, spillway gates, and cranes are inspected on recurring outage cycles. Add Portland-area investment casting plants serving aerospace, railcar and structural steel fabrication, and the Anacortes and Ferndale refineries, and the result is a region that consumes ET, UT, PT/FPI, MT, RT, and VT across two distinct certification frameworks.

sections.heading: Aerospace and the Boeing supply chain: NAS 410 is the gate
paragraphs: Aerospace NDT in Washington and Oregon runs on NAS 410, not on SNT-TC-1A alone — and the difference matters when an employer plans training. NAS 410 requires a documented, syllabus-based training curriculum for each method, sets minimum formal training and experience hours above general-industry recommendations, requires annual near-vision examination, and requires certification to be issued by the employer through a Responsible Level III. A supplier cannot simply send a technician to a generic UT course and call it done; the course content, hours, and examinations must map to the employer's NAS 410 procedure and survive a prime-contractor or Nadcap audit.

The methods aerospace pulls hardest in this region are eddy current — surface and bolt-hole inspection on airframe structures — ultrasonic testing on composites and bond lines, including phased array for wing and fuselage panel work, and fluorescent penetrant inspection at processing houses and casting plants. Radiography concentrates at the casting suppliers around Portland, where investment castings for aerostructures and engines are shot on film and digital systems.

Atlantis NDT delivers NAS 410-compliant method training with the curriculum documentation an auditor expects, and its ASNT Level III consultants can act as the outside examination and Level III resource for suppliers that do not employ their own. For the full aerospace training pathway — methods, hour structures, and how employer certification works under NAS 410 — see the aerospace NDT training page, which pairs with this regional view.

sections.heading: Puget Sound shipyards and naval work
paragraphs: Shipyard NDT around Puget Sound is weld-inspection work at its core: magnetic particle testing on hull and structural welds, ultrasonic thickness surveys on plate and piping, straight-beam and angle-beam UT on butt welds, and visual inspection throughout. Naval availability work at Bremerton and at contractor yards adds a layer of program-specific requirements — NAVSEA technical publications govern personnel qualification and acceptance standards on naval contracts, and technicians moving from commercial to naval work need their certification records and written practice alignment reviewed before they can be badged onto the job.

For employers, the practical training question is throughput: yards staff up for availabilities and repair contracts, and a cohort of trainees needs Level I and Level II method training compressed around production schedules. Atlantis NDT runs shipyard cohorts on-site — using the yard's own consumables, yokes, and UT machines so technicians train on the equipment they will use — or at an arranged venue near the yard when production space is tight. MT and PT are short-cycle methods where a cohort can move from theory to practical examination quickly; UT Level I and Level II each carry roughly 40 hours of formal training under SNT-TC-1A recommendations and are typically scheduled as separate blocks.

sections.heading: Hydro and power infrastructure on the Columbia system
paragraphs: The Columbia and Snake River dams inspect on outage cycles, and outage windows are unforgiving: when a unit comes down, the inspection crew examines turbine runners and blades for cracking with PT and MT, surveys penstock shells with UT thickness grids, inspects spillway gates, trunnions, and lifting equipment, and documents everything against ASME and AWS D1.1 acceptance criteria before the unit returns to service. Federal operators, public utility districts, and their contractors all carry NDT personnel for this work, certified under SNT-TC-1A written practices.

Hydro is also where the Pacific Northwest's aging-infrastructure problem shows up as training demand. Much of the dam fleet dates to the mid-twentieth century, and recurring penstock and gate inspection programs need technicians with strong UT thickness and corrosion-mapping skills plus MT for weld and casting surfaces. Atlantis NDT trains these method combinations as a single cohort program for utility and contractor crews, scheduled against outage calendars rather than a fixed course catalog — theory online in the weeks before the outage, practical on-site with the crew's own equipment.

sections.heading: Methods, hours, and certification frameworks the region pulls
paragraphs: Two frameworks govern nearly all Pacific Northwest NDT certification. General industry — shipyards, hydro, fabrication, refining — runs on SNT-TC-1A: the employer writes a written practice, sets training and experience hours guided by SNT-TC-1A's recommended tables, and certifies its own technicians after documented examinations. Under those recommendations, UT carries about 40 hours of formal training at each of Level I and Level II, with recommended initial experience on the order of 210 hours for Level I and 630 for Level II in the method; surface methods like MT and PT carry substantially fewer training hours, which is why shipyard cohorts often certify MT/PT first and build UT capability second.

Aerospace runs on NAS 410, which raises the floor: a documented curriculum, higher minimum hours, annual vision exams, and a Responsible Level III who owns the program. The regional pattern that follows is predictable — ET and FPI demand clusters in the aerospace corridor at rates well above national averages, while MT and UT thickness demand clusters at the water and the dams. Advertised pay in the region reflects the aerospace premium: Level II ET and FPI postings in the Puget Sound corridor commonly advertise in the low-$30s to high-$40s per hour, above typical general-industry Level II rates. Employers planning a training investment should match the framework to the contract first, then choose methods — the same UT course does not satisfy both frameworks without the right curriculum documentation behind it.

paragraphs: Atlantis NDT delivers Pacific Northwest training three ways, all built around employer cohorts rather than a fixed schoolhouse. Third, blended: the theory portion delivered online, completed around production schedules, followed by a concentrated in-person practical block and examinations.

The blended model matters most in this region because aerospace suppliers rarely release technicians for two consecutive weeks. Splitting UT theory into online modules and compressing the hands-on scanning, calibration, and practical examination into a short on-site block keeps production staffed while the cohort progresses. Examinations — general, specific, and practical — are administered by Atlantis NDT's ASNT Level III consultants and documented for the employer's certification files, whether the framework is SNT-TC-1A or NAS 410. faq.a: SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice: the employer writes its own written practice and sets hours guided by recommended tables. sections.heading: What drives NDT demand in the Permian Basin
paragraphs: The Permian Basin around Midland and Odessa is the highest-output oil-producing region in the United States, and its NDT demand tracks the equipment that production runs through. Every barrel moves through steel that corrodes, threads that wear, and welds that carry pressure: flowlines and gathering systems, tank batteries and saltwater disposal facilities, gas plants and compressor stations, drill strings rotating downhole, and the frac iron and pressure-control equipment cycling between jobs. Each of those asset classes carries a recurring inspection requirement, and together they support one of the densest concentrations of NDT service companies in the country.

The demand profile is different from coastal industrial markets in two ways that shape training. First, it is overwhelmingly an SNT-TC-1A market — service companies certify their own technicians under employer written practices, and the methods are the oilfield workhorses: UT thickness, MT, PT, VT, electromagnetic inspection of tubulars, and RT or phased array on pipeline welds. Second, the workforce runs on rotation schedules, which turns certification into a logistics problem: training blocks, examinations, and on-the-job hour logging all have to fit around hitches. This page is the employer's view of that problem across the basin; the NDT training Midland and NDT training Odessa city pages carry the town-level detail.

sections.heading: UT thickness and asset integrity: the basin's volume method
paragraphs: Ultrasonic thickness testing is the Permian's bread-and-butter method. Corrosion in produced-water service, CO2 floods, and sour systems drives continuous thickness-survey programs on piping circuits, vessels, tanks, and flowlines — condition monitoring locations read on schedule, corrosion rates trended, and repair decisions made from the data. A Level II UT technician who can set up a corrosion survey, grid-map a corroded shell, and document readings cleanly is the single most employable NDT profile in the basin, and service companies build entire crews around that capability.

The certification boundary matters here and is stated plainly: the inspectors who evaluate that data under pressure-vessel, piping, and tank integrity programs often hold API 510, 570, or 653 credentials — and Atlantis NDT does not sell training for those API Individual Certification Program credentials. What Atlantis trains is the NDT capability underneath: UT Level I and Level II under the employer's SNT-TC-1A written practice, where recommendations run roughly 40 hours of formal training at each level with recommended initial experience on the order of 210 hours for Level I and 630 hours for Level II in the method. In the Permian those experience hours accumulate fast — a technician running thickness surveys full-time on rotation logs method hours at a rate few other markets can match.

sections.heading: Tubular and drill-string inspection at the pipe yards
paragraphs: Midland and Odessa host a permanent cluster of pipe yards and tubular inspection facilities, because drill strings and OCTG are inspected between wells the way aircraft are inspected between flights. Used drill pipe comes off a job and runs through electromagnetic inspection (EMI) units that scan the tube body for wall loss, pitting, and transverse defects; end areas and upsets get wet fluorescent MT; tool joints get thread inspection and dimensional gauging; and wall thickness is verified ultrasonically. The governing framework for drill-stem work is the DS-1 standard plus customer specifications, layered over SNT-TC-1A-based personnel certification.

For a tubular inspection employer, the training profile is specific: technicians need MT with wet fluorescent technique, UT wall-measurement capability, EMI unit operation and interpretation, and disciplined visual and dimensional inspection — usually built as a combined program rather than isolated method courses. Atlantis NDT trains these combinations at the yard, on the employer's own EMI line, benches, and pipe racks, so the practical portion happens on the exact equipment and pipe the crew inspects daily. Examinations are administered by ASNT Level III consultants and documented against the employer's written practice, giving yard operators certification files that stand up when a drilling contractor or operator audits the facility.

sections.heading: Pipeline construction and integrity work across the basin
paragraphs: Pipeline NDT in the Permian runs on two tracks. New construction — gathering systems chasing new pads, and transmission lines carrying crude, gas, and NGLs out of the basin — pulls girth-weld inspection on right-of-way spreads: radiography crews shooting welds behind the welding crews, and increasingly phased array and automated UT as operators accept advanced ultrasonics against API 1104 weld acceptance criteria. The second track is integrity: in-line-inspection tools flag anomalies, and dig crews expose the pipe for direct examination — UT thickness and lamination scans, MT and PT on the exposed weld and body, and documentation feeding the operator's integrity-management program.

Both tracks reward the same training investment: conventional UT as the foundation, then phased array as the differentiator. The basin's shift from film radiography toward phased array on girth welds is the clearest capability gap in the regional workforce, and service companies that build phased-array benches win spread work that film-only competitors cannot bid. Atlantis NDT trains that pathway in sequence — UT Level II first, then phased array as an additional qualification under the same written practice — with practical training on girth-weld samples and the employer's own instruments, scheduled between spread mobilizations rather than against a fixed course calendar.

sections.heading: OJT-hour logging on rotation schedules: the Permian certification mechanic
paragraphs: The Permian's defining training constraint is the hitch. Crews work rotation schedules — commonly patterns like 14 days on and 7 off — and any certification program that ignores that rhythm fails in practice. The mechanism that makes SNT-TC-1A certification work on rotation is disciplined on-the-job-training hour logging: the trainee records method-specific hours daily, per method, on a log the supervising Level II or supervisor verifies; the log distinguishes hours actually spent performing and observing the method from general site time; and the employer's certification file accumulates those verified hours until the written practice's experience requirement is met and the practical examination can be scheduled.

Done properly, rotation work is an advantage, not an obstacle. A trainee running thickness surveys twelve hours a day on hitch banks method hours at two to three times the rate of a forty-hour-week technician elsewhere, which is why Permian trainees routinely reach experience thresholds in fewer calendar months than the national norm. The failure mode is equally common: hours never logged, logged in bulk at month-end, or logged without method breakdown — records that collapse under audit and force certifications to be rebuilt. Atlantis NDT sets up the logging system as part of every Permian training program: log formats matched to the written practice, supervisor verification routines, and periodic Level III review of the files, so the hours a crew actually works convert into certifications that survive scrutiny.

paragraphs: The Permian pays for certified capability because uncertified capability cannot bill. Advertised postings for Level II UT technicians in the Midland-Odessa market commonly run from the high-$20s into the $40s per hour depending on methods carried, with day-rate and per-diem structures on pipeline and turnaround work pushing effective earnings higher; phased-array capability commands the top of the band. Those are advertised-market observations, not a rate card — but they explain the economics of training: a service company that certifies a trainee into a billable Level II converts a cost line into a revenue line, and the rotation schedule shortens the calendar time that conversion takes.

For an employer building a bench, the sequence that works in this basin: start trainees logging hours from their first hitch, train and certify the surface methods and VT early for broad crew utility, build UT Level II as the core billable capability, then layer EMI or phased array according to the yard's book of work. Where the company has no Level III on staff — the common case among Permian service companies — Atlantis NDT provides the outsourced ASNT Level III who authors the written practice, administers examinations, reviews the OJT logs, and answers the auditor. That standing Level III layer plus yard-delivered training is how a Midland or Odessa service company builds a certification program that scales with the rig count instead of scrambling behind it.

h1: NDT Training Across the Great Lakes Industrial Corridor
answer: Great Lakes NDT training demand comes from four employer groups: automotive manufacturing centred on Detroit, integrated steel from Gary through Cleveland, shipbuilding at Marinette and Sturgeon Bay, and the nuclear and gas power fleet along the lakeshore. The methods that anchor the region are magnetic particle and liquid penetrant testing at production volume, ultrasonic testing of welds, castings and mill product, and visual weld inspection under AWS D1.1.
expansion: The corridor's advantage for an employer building an in-house NDT capability is density. Certification in the United States is employer-based under ASNT SNT-TC-1A: the company's own Written Practice governs training hours, experience and examinations, and a Level III administers the programme. Because the Great Lakes packs automotive plants, steel mills, fabrication shops, shipyards and power stations into one commuting geography, the same cohort model repeats from a Detroit stamping plant to a Milwaukee fabricator — only the method mix changes. Automotive pulls production-volume MT and PT plus ultrasonic spot-weld and casting examination; the mills run automated UT and eddy current lines that still need certified people to set up, calibrate and evaluate; the fab belt lives on AWS D1.1; and the shipyards and nuclear stations layer naval and ASME in-service requirements on top of the same Level II foundations. This page maps those sub-markets, links the city pages that sit inside the region, and explains how training is actually delivered across it.
