facets.q: Which NDT method should a Great Lakes fabricator train first?
facets.a: Magnetic particle testing first, then ultrasonic testing. MT covers the highest volume of AWS D1.1 surface examination in a structural shop, the equipment cost is low, and a cohort reaches useful productivity fastest. UT comes second because D1.1 volumetric examination of groove welds is where fabricators most often depend on outside contractors — bringing shear-wave UT in-house is usually the largest single saving an inspection budget can make. PT and VT round out the set; VT is routinely undertrained despite being the method every weld sees.

facets.q: How do AWS CWI inspectors and NDT Level II technicians divide D1.1 work?
facets.a: The Certified Welding Inspector owns visual acceptance and the overall conformance decision under AWS D1.1; NDT Level II technicians perform the UT, MT and PT examinations the code requires and report results against its acceptance criteria. They are separate credentials on separate tracks — a CWI qualification does not confer NDT method certification, and a Level II card does not authorise weld acceptance sign-off. Most Great Lakes fabricators run both: a CWI or Senior CWI over the programme, with employer-certified Level IIs doing method work. Atlantis trains the NDT side and aligns it to the shop's D1.1 workflow.

facets.q: Can a plant run NDT theory online and practicals in person?
facets.a: Yes, and for shift-based Great Lakes plants it is the default Atlantis delivery model. SNT-TC-1A leaves the training format to the employer's Written Practice, so the classroom hours can be satisfied by structured online theory that trainees complete around production schedules, followed by concentrated in-person practical days on calibration blocks, real components and the plant's own instruments. The practical examination and the administered written examinations happen in person under the Level III. The blend cuts line downtime without cutting documented hours.

facets.q: What does SNT-TC-1A require before a technician examines as UT Level II?
facets.a: Three things, all governed by the employer's Written Practice: documented formal training — SNT-TC-1A recommends 40 hours of instruction for UT Level I and a further 40 for Level II; documented experience time in the method accumulated under supervision; and examinations administered by the Level III — general (theory), specific (the employer's procedures) and practical (hands-on demonstration), plus a near-vision acuity check. The recommended figures are the ASNT baseline; the employer's Written Practice states the binding numbers, which is why cohort training is scoped against that document first.

facets.q: What is different about shipyard NDT at Marinette?
facets.a: The qualification bar. Naval construction at Marinette runs to NAVSEA technical publications and military acceptance criteria, which sit on top of — not instead of — a technician's Level II certification. Examiners qualify to specific written procedures, acceptance criteria are tighter than commercial structural work, and the documentation burden is heavier at every step. A Level II certified in a commercial fab shop is not automatically deployable on naval hull work; the yard's programme qualifies them to its procedures. Training for that environment emphasises procedure literacy and records discipline as much as probe skills.

facets.q: Does automated mill inspection remove the need for certified technicians in Gary?
facets.a: No. The automated UT and eddy current lines at the integrated mills around Gary and East Chicago detect and gate product automatically, but certified people set the systems up, calibrate them against reference standards, evaluate flagged indications and disposition product against ASTM and customer specifications. Plate UT to standards such as ASTM A435 or A578 still ends in a human evaluation and a signature. The mills also carry a parallel maintenance-NDT workload — MT and UT on rolls, housings and cranes — that is entirely hands-on. Automation moved the certified work; it did not remove it.

sections.heading: Four employer groups set Great Lakes NDT demand
paragraphs: Automotive around Detroit and Toledo runs the highest inspection volume in the region: resistance spot welds by the thousand per body, structural welds on frames and chassis components, castings and forgings through powertrain and the supplier tiers. Steel at the bottom of Lake Michigan — Gary Works, Indiana Harbor, Burns Harbor — and along the Cuyahoga in Cleveland pulls automated ultrasonic and eddy current examination on product lines plus magnetic particle work on some of the heaviest rotating and structural plant in the country. Shipbuilding at Marinette and Sturgeon Bay adds a naval-standards overlay to the same structural methods. And the lakeshore power fleet — Cook, Palisades, Fermi 2, Davis-Besse and Perry among the nuclear stations, with gas capacity replacing retired coal — buys in-service examination on the outage calendar.

For a training manager, the region's density is the point. Cohorts can be built from people with adjacent industrial experience, supervised experience hours accumulate quickly because examination work is constant, and a certification earned at one plant translates to the next because the whole corridor runs the same SNT-TC-1A employer-based model. The cities inside this region with dedicated pages: Detroit, Chicago, Cleveland, Milwaukee and Gary.

sections.heading: Detroit: production-volume MT and PT, plus the UT that pays for itself
paragraphs: Detroit's plants examine at a volume no other Great Lakes sub-market matches. Body and stamping operations generate continuous surface-examination demand; powertrain castings and forgings pull ultrasonic and radiographic work; and automated eddy current lines screen machined components at line speed. The method economics follow the volume: magnetic particle and penetrant cohorts reach productivity fast, while ultrasonic capability — casting examination, spot-weld evaluation, weld inspection on frames and fixtures — is where plants most often pay outside contractors and where in-house certification pays back hardest. The dedicated pages for the metro cover this in method depth: ultrasonic testing in Detroit and magnetic particle testing in Detroit.

A typical Detroit training engagement is a plant cohort, not individual enrolment: quality and maintenance staff trained together against the plant's Written Practice, theory completed online around shift patterns, practical days run on the plant floor with the components the technicians will actually examine, and examinations administered on-site. Supplier-tier shops run the same model at smaller scale — often starting with MT and VT to bring AWS-regime surface examination in-house, then adding UT as the programme matures. See the Detroit training page for the city-level picture.

sections.heading: Steel from Gary to Cleveland: automated lines still need certified people
paragraphs: The integrated mills from Gary and East Chicago to Burns Harbor, and the steel and forging economy around Cleveland and Lorain, run two distinct examination workloads. The first is product examination: automated ultrasonic and eddy current systems on plate, bar and tube, testing to ASTM standards and customer specifications. Certified technicians set those systems up, calibrate them against reference standards, evaluate flagged indications and disposition product — the automation finds, the Level II decides. The second is maintenance examination: MT and UT on mill rolls, crane hooks, housings and structural steel, which is entirely manual and runs year-round.

Training for mill crews is therefore method-deep rather than method-broad: straight-beam and angle-beam UT taken well past the minimum hours, eddy current theory tied to the specific line configurations the crew operates, and MT for the maintenance department. The steel base also feeds the surrounding fabrication economy, where AWS-regime weld examination is the classic entry environment — the manufacturing NDT training page for Gary covers that pathway from the mill gate outward.

sections.heading: AWS D1.1 is the corridor's common language
paragraphs: From a Milwaukee mining-equipment shop to a Chicago structural fabricator to a Detroit fixture builder, the acceptance criteria on the drawing are AWS D1.1. That shared code is what makes the Great Lakes the easiest US region to build NDT fundamentals in: the visual, magnetic particle, penetrant and ultrasonic skills a technician certifies in at one D1.1 shop transfer to the next with only a Written Practice re-qualification, not a restart. Employers in Chicago and Milwaukee hiring from each other's labour pools is the normal state of the market.

D1.1 also defines the division of labour a training plan has to respect: the Certified Welding Inspector owns visual acceptance and conformance sign-off, while NDT Level II technicians perform the code's UT, MT and PT examinations. Shops that certify their welders, employ or contract a CWI, and train an in-house Level II bench hold the whole quality loop internally. Atlantis trains the NDT side of that loop and aligns it to the shop's D1.1 workflow — the weld inspection page sets out how the method examinations and the acceptance decision fit together.

sections.heading: Shipbuilding at Marinette and the lakeshore power fleet
paragraphs: Marinette, Wisconsin is the Great Lakes' naval yard: Fincantieri Marinette Marine builds surface combatants for the US Navy, and down the shore at Sturgeon Bay, Bay Shipbuilding handles commercial construction and the winter repair of the lakes freighter fleet. Both run structural UT, MT and VT at volume, but the naval work overlays NAVSEA technical publications and military acceptance criteria on the commercial foundation — tighter criteria, procedure-specific examiner qualification, and a documentation standard that commercial fabrication does not prepare a technician for. Training aimed at the yards therefore weights procedure literacy and records discipline equally with probe skills.

The power fleet is the region's other qualification-heavy buyer. The nuclear stations strung along the lakeshore examine on the outage calendar — concentrated windows of UT, MT, PT and VT under ASME Section XI in-service rules — and the Palisades restart campaign in Michigan has added examination demand of a kind the US fleet has not generated before. Gas-fired capacity replacing retired coal adds ASME construction and maintenance examination on top. The power generation NDT training page covers the qualification ladder that work sits on.

sections.heading: How training is delivered across the Great Lakes
paragraphs: Atlantis NDT does not operate a training centre in the region, and for employer cohorts that is the right answer anyway: training is delivered on-site at the plant, shipyard or mill, or at an arranged venue — a hotel conference facility or rented training room provisioned with calibration blocks, test specimens and instruments — close to where the cohort works. Theory is delivered online, self-paced, completed around production schedules; practical hours, practical examinations and the administered written examinations happen in person. For a multi-plant employer, one arranged venue can serve cohorts drawn from Detroit, Toledo and Cleveland in a single mobilisation.

On-site delivery has a second advantage the classroom cannot match: practical training runs on the components, procedures and instruments the technicians will actually use, so the practical examination demonstrates the real job rather than a generic one. Scheduling follows the plant, not the calendar — around shutdown windows in the mills, model changeovers in automotive, and outage seasons in power.

sections.heading: Certification mechanics: SNT-TC-1A and the outsourced Level III
paragraphs: Every corridor in this region certifies the same way: employer-based certification under ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The employer holds a Written Practice defining training hours, experience requirements and examination standards for each method and level; technicians accumulate documented training and supervised experience against it; and an NDT Level III administers the general, specific and practical examinations and recommends certification. The certification belongs to the employer — which is why cohort training scoped against the Written Practice, rather than open-enrolment coursework, is how Great Lakes plants actually build capability.

Most manufacturers and fabricators in the region do not employ a Level III, and do not need to. Atlantis NDT provides the full loop as a service: authoring or updating the Written Practice, delivering the blended training, administering examinations, and providing ongoing outsourced Level III coverage for procedure approval, technician certification and audit support. Scope is quoted on request against the methods, levels and headcount involved.

faq.q: Does Atlantis NDT have a training centre in Detroit, Cleveland or Chicago?
faq.a: No. Training across the Great Lakes is delivered on-site at the employer's plant, mill or yard, or at an arranged venue near the cohort, with theory completed online and practical hours and examinations conducted in person. There are no fixed Atlantis premises in the region, and none are needed for the employer-cohort model.

faq.q: Does Atlantis sell API 510, 570 or 653 training?
faq.a: No. Atlantis NDT does not offer API 510, API 570 or API 653 certification training. We train the NDT methods — UT, MT, PT, RT, VT and the advanced techniques — that feed inspection programmes governed by those codes, and we provide outsourced Level III support to the contractors and owners running them.

faq.q: How large should an on-site cohort be?
faq.a: Cohorts of roughly four to twelve technicians work best: large enough to justify mobilising instructors and equipment to your site, small enough that every trainee gets sustained instrument time. Mixed-method programmes — for example MT plus UT across one visit — are common. Scope and scheduling are quoted on request.

faq.q: Which city pages sit inside the Great Lakes region?
faq.a: Dedicated training pages exist for Detroit, Chicago, Cleveland, Milwaukee and Gary, with method-level pages including ultrasonic testing in Detroit and manufacturing NDT training in Gary. Marinette and Sturgeon Bay shipyard work is covered on this page.

faq.q: How long does it take to get a new hire working as a Level II?
faq.a: The formal training weeks are the fast part; the supervised experience hours defined in the employer's Written Practice are the schedule driver, and they accumulate at the pace of real examination work. In a high-volume Great Lakes plant a trainee logs hours quickly, but plan in months, not weeks — and plan the Level I stage as productive time, since Level I technicians perform examinations under supervision.

title: NDT Training Mid-Atlantic — Naval Shipbuilding, Refining & the Port
description: NDT training across the Mid-Atlantic: Newport News and Norfolk naval shipbuilding, Delaware Valley refining, Baltimore's port and bridge steel — delivered on-site to employer cohorts.
h1: NDT Training Across the Mid-Atlantic Corridor
answer: Mid-Atlantic NDT training demand splits three ways: naval shipbuilding and repair at Newport News and Norfolk, in-service inspection across the Delaware Valley refining corridor around Philadelphia, and Baltimore's port, ship-repair and bridge-steel economy. Naval standards set the region's qualification bar — NAVSEA technical publications and military acceptance criteria layered over conventional Level II certification — and that bar bleeds outward into what every employer in the corridor expects from documentation.
expansion: No US region concentrates naval examination work like Hampton Roads. Newport News Shipbuilding is the country's only builder of nuclear-powered aircraft carriers and one of its two submarine builders; across the water, Norfolk Naval Shipyard and the private repair yards run fleet maintenance on a continuous drydock tempo. That industrial base employs UT, RT, MT, PT and VT at scale under the strictest qualification regime in American industry, and it anchors a supply chain of fabricators and inspection contractors that certify to the same expectations. North of it, the Delaware Valley's operating refineries — Trainer, Paulsboro, Delaware City — buy turnaround and on-stream inspection governed by API in-service codes, while Baltimore adds port infrastructure, the Coast Guard Yard at Curtis Bay, ship repair at Sparrows Point and the Key Bridge rebuild's structural steel. For a training buyer the region rewards one thing above all: technicians who document to the naval standard, because that credibility travels down the entire seaboard.

facets.q: Do naval shipyard NDT qualifications transfer to commercial work?
facets.a: Downward, yes; upward, no. A technician qualified to naval procedures at Newport News or Norfolk walks into commercial structural or marine work with a documentation habit and method rigour that employers read as a premium — the naval standard is the ceiling of the market. The reverse transfer does not hold: a commercially certified Level II is not deployable on naval scope until qualified to the yard's specific procedures under its programme. Training aimed at yard supply-chain work therefore builds SNT-TC-1A certification to survive yard audit from day one.

facets.q: What does a refinery turnaround pull from a Philadelphia-area inspection contractor?
facets.a: Volume UT first: corrosion-monitoring thickness surveys across piping circuits and vessels, executed and documented fast during the outage window. Then profile radiography on insulated small-bore piping, MT and PT on repair welds as they complete, and advanced ultrasonics where dead legs and damage mechanisms demand it. The programmes are governed by API in-service codes, but what the contractor certifies its technicians in is the NDT methods — which is exactly the training Atlantis delivers, scoped to the contractor's Written Practice ahead of turnaround season at Trainer, Paulsboro or Delaware City.

facets.q: Does Atlantis train technicians to NAVSEA standards?
facets.a: Atlantis trains and certifies the method foundation — UT, RT, MT, PT, VT under SNT-TC-1A — that naval qualification is built on, and builds cohort programmes to the documentation standard yard flow-downs demand. Qualification to specific NAVSEA procedures and acceptance criteria is administered by the yard or the prime contractor under its own programme; no outside trainer confers it. The practical division: we get a supplier's technicians certified, procedure-literate and audit-ready; the yard's programme qualifies them to its procedures.

facets.q: Which methods should a Baltimore structural fabricator certify first?
facets.a: Visual and magnetic particle first — they cover the bulk of AWS D1.1 surface examination on port, building and bridge steel — then shear-wave UT, which is where fabricators most depend on subcontracted inspection. Bridge work adds a wrinkle: AWS D1.5 governs bridge welding, with its own examination requirements, and the Key Bridge rebuild has made D1.5-regime capability a live differentiator for Baltimore shops. A three-method cohort — VT, MT, UT — trained on-site against the shop's Written Practice is the standard starting scope.

facets.q: Can shift crews at a yard or refinery do theory online?
facets.a: Yes — that is the standard Atlantis delivery for the Mid-Atlantic's shift-based employers. SNT-TC-1A lets the employer's Written Practice define how training hours are delivered, so theory runs as structured online coursework completed around watch and shift schedules, and instructors mobilise for concentrated practical days at the site or an arranged venue nearby. Practical training uses representative specimens and the employer's instruments; written and practical examinations are administered in person by the Level III. Crews stay on shift; the training record stays complete.

facets.q: Why does certification earned in Hampton Roads travel so well?
facets.a: Because the region's reference standard is the naval one. NAVSEA technical publications and MIL-standard acceptance criteria demand procedure-specific qualification and record-keeping beyond anything commercial codes require, and every fabricator and contractor in the yards' supply chain absorbs that expectation through purchase-order flow-downs. A technician whose certification file was built to survive a yard audit — complete training records, documented experience, examinations traceable to a Written Practice — clears any commercial employer's review on the spot. Employers along the whole East Coast read Hampton Roads paperwork as a proxy for rigour.

sections.heading: Three economies, one certification corridor
paragraphs: The Mid-Atlantic runs three distinct examination economies within three hours' drive of each other. Hampton Roads is naval: Newport News Shipbuilding constructing carriers and submarines, Norfolk Naval Shipyard and the private yards maintaining the Atlantic fleet, and a fabrication supply chain certified to their flow-downs. The Delaware Valley is process: the operating refineries at Trainer, Paulsboro and Delaware City buying turnaround and on-stream inspection year-round. Baltimore is structural and marine: port infrastructure, the Coast Guard Yard at Curtis Bay, ship repair at Sparrows Point, and the bridge-steel workload the Key Bridge rebuild has concentrated there.

What unifies them is the certification model and the standard-setter. All three certify under employer-based SNT-TC-1A, and the naval regime at the region's core sets a documentation bar the whole corridor feels. The cities inside this region with dedicated pages: Norfolk, Newport News, Philadelphia and Baltimore.

sections.heading: Newport News: the deepest qualification bar in American industry
paragraphs: Newport News Shipbuilding is the only yard in the country that builds nuclear-powered aircraft carriers and one of two that build nuclear submarines, and its examination regime matches the product: UT, RT, MT, PT and VT executed to NAVSEA technical publications and MIL-standard acceptance criteria, with naval nuclear overlays on reactor-plant work. Examiners qualify to specific procedures, not just methods; acceptance criteria run tighter than any commercial code; and every examination lives or dies by its documentation. The Newport News training page covers the city market, maritime NDT training in Newport News the shipyard pathway, and nuclear NDT training in Newport News the reactor-plant overlay.

For employers, the yard's scale shapes the whole regional labour market: it trains continuously, its supply chain must certify to its flow-downs, and its alumni set the standard everywhere they land. A fabricator or inspection contractor selling into that supply chain wins or loses on whether its SNT-TC-1A programme survives yard audit — which is precisely the outcome a cohort programme and outsourced Level III support are scoped to deliver.

sections.heading: Norfolk and Portsmouth: repair tempo and the maritime pathway
paragraphs: Across Hampton Roads from the construction yard, the repair economy runs on availability schedules: Norfolk Naval Shipyard in Portsmouth — one of the Navy's four public shipyards — plus the private repair yards working surface ships against NAVSEA Standard Items. Repair NDT is different work from new construction: thickness surveys on aged structure, MT and PT on repair welds under schedule pressure, VT everywhere, and findings that feed directly into work-package decisions. Cohort training for repair contractors weights UT thickness and structural examination and the records discipline the Standard Items regime demands. The Norfolk training page and maritime NDT training in Norfolk cover the city-level market.

The career and cohort pathway for the whole waterfront — which methods to certify first for ship work, how class-society and naval requirements differ, and how a marine technician's certification file should be built — is laid out on the maritime NDT training page. For Mid-Atlantic employers it is the natural companion to this one: the region page says where the work is; the maritime page says how the qualification ladder is climbed.

sections.heading: Delaware Valley refining: method training that feeds API programmes
paragraphs: Refining around Philadelphia consolidated after the 2019 Philadelphia Energy Solutions closure, but the corridor still operates: Monroe Energy's Trainer refinery, PBF's Paulsboro and Delaware City plants. Their inspection programmes are governed by API in-service codes, and the demand they generate for training is method demand: UT corrosion-monitoring surveys at turnaround volume, profile radiography on insulated piping, MT and PT on repair welds, and advanced ultrasonics on known damage mechanisms. Contractors staff up against turnaround calendars, and the constraint is almost always certified UT hands. City-level method pages cover the metro: ultrasonic testing in Philadelphia and radiographic testing in Philadelphia, alongside the Philadelphia training page.

One boundary stated plainly: Atlantis NDT does not sell API 510, 570 or 653 certification training. What we train is the NDT bench those API-governed programmes depend on — Level I and II method certification under the contractor's Written Practice, delivered before the season, plus outsourced Level III coverage for procedures and examinations. The API inspector credential and the NDT technician certification are different roles, and the region needs far more of the second.

sections.heading: Baltimore: port steel, ship repair and a bridge to rebuild
paragraphs: Baltimore's examination economy is structural. The port's cranes and infrastructure carry recurring weld and thickness examination; the Coast Guard Yard at Curtis Bay runs cutter maintenance; Tradepoint Atlantic's redevelopment of Sparrows Point has brought ship repair and heavy industrial work back to the old Bethlehem Steel ground; and the Francis Scott Key Bridge rebuild has made bridge-code steel the region's marquee workload. Structural work in the harbor runs to AWS D1.1; the bridge work runs to AWS D1.5, the Bridge Welding Code, whose examination requirements shape what fabricators and erection contractors must certify for.

For Baltimore fabricators and contractors the standard cohort is VT, MT and shear-wave UT trained against the shop's Written Practice — the combination that covers D1.1 surface and volumetric examination and positions a shop for bridge-regime work. The Baltimore training page carries the city-level detail.

sections.heading: The nuclear arc: outage examination from Calvert Cliffs to Limerick
paragraphs: Ringing the region's north and east is a dense nuclear fleet: Calvert Cliffs on the Chesapeake, Salem and Hope Creek on the Delaware, Peach Bottom and Limerick in Pennsylvania. Their in-service examination runs under ASME Section XI on the outage calendar — concentrated spring and fall windows when qualified UT, MT, PT and VT technicians are pulled into the sites in numbers. For inspection contractors the fleet is a scheduling business: certifications, vision examinations and site-access requirements must all be current before the window opens, because nothing is fixable once it does.

Training for outage crews is therefore cyclical: recertification and refresher training in the shoulder seasons, near-vision examinations on schedule, and method top-ups where a site's scope demands techniques a technician has not exercised recently. An outsourced Level III keeps that machine running — tracking certification expiries against outage dates and administering examinations before crews mobilise.

sections.heading: How training is delivered across the Mid-Atlantic
paragraphs: Atlantis NDT operates no training premises in the region. Delivery is on-site at the yard, plant, or shop, or at an arranged venue — a rented training room provisioned with specimens, calibration standards and instruments — placed where the cohort is: Hampton Roads for the marine trades, the Delaware Valley for refinery contractors, Baltimore for the structural shops. Theory is delivered online and self-paced, which matters in a region where cohorts work watches, shifts and outage rotations; practical training, practical examinations and administered written examinations happen in person.

The employer-cohort model fits this region better than any classroom could, because the qualification target differs by employer: a yard supplier trains to survive naval audit, a turnaround contractor trains for speed and volume, a bridge fabricator trains to D1.5. Scoping starts from the employer's Written Practice and flow-down requirements, and the programme — methods, levels, hours, examinations — is built against that. Scope and scheduling are quoted on request.

sections.heading: Certification mechanics: SNT-TC-1A under a naval shadow
paragraphs: The whole corridor certifies under employer-based SNT-TC-1A — Written Practice, documented training and experience, Level III-administered examinations — but the naval presence changes how well the paperwork must be kept. Yard flow-downs and government audits probe certification files at a depth commercial work never does, and the regional habit that results is the Mid-Atlantic's quiet competitive advantage: records built here clear reviews everywhere.

Most fabricators, repair contractors and inspection firms in the region do not employ a Level III. Atlantis provides the function as a service: Written Practice authorship and maintenance, blended training delivery, examination administration, certification recommendation, and standing support for audits and procedure approval. For employers selling into the yards or staffing the refinery and outage calendars, that is the piece that turns trained technicians into a certifiable, auditable programme.

faq.q: Does Atlantis NDT have a training centre in Norfolk, Philadelphia or Baltimore?
faq.a: No. Mid-Atlantic training is delivered on-site at the employer's yard, plant or shop, or at an arranged venue near the cohort, with theory online and practical hours and examinations in person. Atlantis maintains no fixed premises in the region; the employer-cohort model does not need them.

faq.q: Does Atlantis sell API 510, 570 or 653 training?
faq.a: No. Atlantis NDT does not offer API 510, API 570 or API 653 certification courses. For the Delaware Valley refining market we train the NDT methods — UT, RT, MT, PT, VT and advanced techniques — that API-governed inspection programmes consume, and we provide outsourced Level III support to the contractors running them.

faq.q: Can you certify our technicians for work inside the Navy yards?
faq.a: We certify technicians under your SNT-TC-1A Written Practice and build the training and records to the standard naval flow-downs demand. Qualification to specific NAVSEA procedures is administered by the yard or prime contractor under its own programme — no external trainer confers it. Our role is delivering technicians whose method certification and documentation are ready for that step.

faq.q: Which city pages sit inside the Mid-Atlantic region?
faq.a: Dedicated pages cover Norfolk, Newport News, Philadelphia and Baltimore, with specialised pages for maritime NDT training in Norfolk, maritime NDT training in Newport News and nuclear NDT training in Newport News. The regional maritime pathway is on the maritime NDT training page.

faq.q: When should a turnaround contractor schedule training?
faq.a: In the shoulder seasons, before the spring and fall turnaround and outage windows. Certification, recertification and vision examinations must all be complete before mobilisation, and training a cohort mid-season is effectively impossible. Contractors typically scope winter and mid-summer deliveries; Atlantis schedules against your season, quoted on request.

title: NDT Training Appalachia — Marcellus, Pipeline Integrity & Steel
description: NDT training across Appalachia: Marcellus and Utica gathering and midstream, pipeline integrity digs, the Monaca cracker and Pittsburgh's steel base — delivered on-site to crews and cohorts.
h1: NDT Training Across Appalachia's Gas and Steel Corridor
answer: Appalachian NDT training demand is pipeline-led: Marcellus and Utica gas gathering, midstream processing and transmission integrity work across Pennsylvania, West Virginia and eastern Ohio, layered over Pittsburgh's steel and fabrication base. Ultrasonic testing is the anchor method — girth-weld examination during construction under API 1104, and wall-thickness verification on the integrity digs that in-line MFL inspection generates — with magnetic particle testing close behind and radiography still standard on tie-ins.
expansion: The Marcellus and Utica shales turned Appalachia into one of the largest gas-producing regions on earth, and the examination economy follows the molecules: gathering systems and compressor stations across southwest Pennsylvania and the West Virginia panhandle, cryogenic processing and fractionation complexes in the wet-gas window, transmission lines carrying the gas out of the basin, and the Shell Polymers Monaca complex converting ethane at the basin's northern edge. Pipeline work splits into two NDT workloads with different rhythms: construction examination of girth welds to API 1104 as new pipe goes in, and integrity verification — the dig programmes that follow in-line inspection runs — on everything already buried. Underneath the gas economy sits the older one: US Steel's Mon Valley Works, the specialty metals producers, and the fabricators that grew up around Pittsburgh steel. This page maps those sub-markets, links the city and state pages inside the region, and explains how training reaches crews spread across a three-state basin.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does a pipeline dig crew need?
facets.a: Ultrasonic testing and magnetic particle testing, plus disciplined visual examination. When an in-line inspection run flags metal loss or a dent, the dig crew's job is to characterise it: UT thickness grids and corrosion mapping over the flagged area, pit-depth gauging, MT on dents, gouges and adjacent girth welds to find cracking the tools cannot classify, and documentation formatted to feed the operator's ASME B31.8S integrity assessment. RT rarely comes to a dig. A two-method UT/MT Level II with strong reporting habits is the complete dig technician, and that is the standard Atlantis crew package for the basin.

facets.q: Is MFL something a field technician certifies in?
facets.a: Not in the SNT-TC-1A field sense. Magnetic flux leakage in-line inspection is run by the ILI vendors — the tools are theirs, and the data analysts who grade the signals qualify under the vendors' own programmes and industry practice for ILI personnel. What the field side certifies in is the verification work MFL generates: when the operator digs on an ILI call, certified UT and MT technicians measure the real condition, and their results are what the tool's performance is judged against. Field crews need to read ILI dig sheets fluently; they do not need to run the tool.

facets.q: RT or phased array for girth welds?
facets.a: Both are in service across Appalachia, and the direction of travel is toward automated and phased array ultrasonics. Radiography remains standard on tie-ins and on spreads where the contract specifies it, but AUT crews pace mainline production welding faster, deliver height-sized flaw data that supports engineering critical assessment under API 1104's alternative acceptance provisions, and carry no source-radiation exclusion zones. For a training buyer the practical answer: certify the bench in conventional UT first — it is the prerequisite skill — then qualify selected technicians on the phased array procedures the operators are specifying.

facets.q: How does Operator Qualification differ from NDT certification?
facets.a: They answer different regulators. Operator Qualification is the PHMSA-driven requirement under 49 CFR 192 and 195 that individuals performing covered tasks on regulated pipelines demonstrate qualification on those tasks — it attaches to tasks like coating inspection or pipe handling, and it is managed through OQ providers and operator programmes. NDT certification under SNT-TC-1A is the employer-based method qualification — UT, MT, RT — that governs examination work itself. A pipeline NDT technician in the Marcellus typically needs both: OQ to be on the right-of-way, method certification to put a probe on the weld.

facets.q: What training does the Appalachian midstream buildout pull?
facets.a: Plant-side methods on an ASME footing. The cryogenic processing and fractionation complexes in the West Virginia panhandle and eastern Ohio were built — and are maintained — under ASME Section VIII and B31.3 rules, so the examination workload is UT on vessels and piping, RT and advanced UT on critical welds, and MT/PT through maintenance cycles. It behaves like refinery work with a gas accent: turnaround windows, contractor crews, certification current before mobilisation. The oil and gas NDT training page covers the method ladder for this work; the West Virginia page covers the state market.

facets.q: Can field crews do theory online between spreads?
facets.a: Yes — for a workforce scattered across a three-state basin it is the only model that works. Theory is delivered as structured online coursework technicians complete from home or camp between spreads, on a schedule the Written Practice documents; instructors then mobilise for concentrated practical days at the contractor's yard or an arranged venue near the work — calibration blocks, pipe specimens with real flaws, the crew's own instruments. Written and practical examinations are administered in person by the Level III. Crews lose days to training, not weeks, and the certification file is complete.

sections.heading: Gas underfoot sets the training agenda
paragraphs: The Marcellus and Utica made Appalachia a gas province on a world scale, and the NDT economy tracks the infrastructure: gathering systems and compressor stations across southwest Pennsylvania's Washington and Greene county core, cryogenic processing and fractionation in the West Virginia panhandle and eastern Ohio's wet-gas window, transmission capacity carrying the basin's output to market, and the Shell Polymers Monaca complex cracking ethane at the northern edge. Every one of those assets was welded into existence under examination, and every buried mile of it now generates integrity work for as long as it operates.

Two older economies sit underneath. Pittsburgh's steel base — the Mon Valley Works, the specialty metals producers, the fabricators — remains the region's traditional NDT entry point. And the Kanawha Valley's chemical plants around Charleston keep a steady in-service examination demand in West Virginia's south. The pages inside this region: Pittsburgh at city level and West Virginia at state level, with this page carrying the basin-wide view.

sections.heading: Girth welds: API 1104 and the shift from film to phased array
paragraphs: Construction examination in the basin runs to API 1104, Welding of Pipelines and Related Facilities — the code that governs girth-weld acceptance on the gathering and transmission systems. The traditional workflow is radiographic: RT crews chasing the welding spread, shooting and reading film or digital images against 1104 acceptance criteria. That workflow still runs, especially on tie-ins, but automated and phased array ultrasonics have been taking mainline production share for years — AUT paces faster welding, sizes flaw height in a way film cannot, supports the engineering-critical-assessment route to acceptance that API 1104 provides for, and removes radiation exclusion zones from the right-of-way.

The training consequence is a layered bench. Conventional UT Level II is the foundation — it is both a working qualification in its own right and the prerequisite for the phased array procedures operators increasingly specify. RT capability remains worth holding for tie-in and contract-specified work. Atlantis builds contractor cohorts in exactly that order: conventional UT and MT as the base, RT where the contractor's market demands it, and phased array qualification for the technicians who will run the automated systems.

sections.heading: Integrity digs: where MFL stops and certified hands take over
paragraphs: Everything already buried generates the basin's second workload. Operators run in-line inspection tools — magnetic flux leakage for metal loss, caliper for geometry — through their transmission systems under the integrity-management requirements of 49 CFR 192 and 195 and the framework of ASME B31.8S. The tools produce call lists; the call lists produce digs; and at the bottom of every dig is a certified NDT crew verifying what the tool reported. That verification is hands-on: UT thickness grids and corrosion mapping across the flagged region, pit gauging, MT on dents, gouges and girth welds, and reporting formatted so the operator's integrity engineers can close the assessment.

MFL itself is not a field certification — the ILI vendors run the tools and qualify their own analysts — but a dig technician must read ILI dig sheets fluently and understand what the tool can and cannot discriminate, because the field measurement is the ground truth the whole programme calibrates against. Dig-crew training is therefore a package: UT and MT method certification under the contractor's Written Practice, plus the integrity-context literacy that makes the crew's documentation immediately usable. It is the most repeatable training product in the basin, because dig programmes run every construction off-season.

sections.heading: Midstream plants and the Monaca cracker
paragraphs: The processing layer between wellhead and market — cryogenic plants, fractionators, compression and storage — was built under ASME Section VIII and B31.3 and is examined under the owners' inspection programmes through maintenance and turnaround cycles. The workload profiles like refinery inspection: volume UT on vessels and piping circuits, RT and advanced UT on critical welds, MT and PT trailing repair work, all of it concentrated into outage windows that punish any crew whose certifications are not current before mobilisation. At the basin's northern edge, the Shell Polymers Monaca complex adds a world-scale petrochemical site with a standing maintenance-examination demand of its own.

For contractors serving this layer, the training rhythm is seasonal: certify and recertify in the shoulder months, examine in the windows. The method ladder for the whole oil and gas vertical — which methods, which order, and how the in-service world differs from construction — is laid out on the oil and gas NDT training page; plant-market detail for the panhandle sits on the West Virginia training page.

sections.heading: Pittsburgh: the steel legacy still trains technicians
paragraphs: Before the basin had gas money it had steel, and the steel economy still anchors the region's method depth. US Steel's Mon Valley Works — Clairton, Edgar Thomson, Irvin — the specialty metals producers, and the structural fabricators around Pittsburgh run the classic manufacturing examination set: UT on forgings and product, MT at maintenance volume, RT on critical welds, all under AWS D1.1 and ASTM product standards. It is the region's traditional Level I/II entry environment, and it feeds the gas economy directly — a technician who learned shear-wave UT in a Pittsburgh fab shop is a short qualification step from girth-weld work.

The city's method pages carry the detail: ultrasonic testing in Pittsburgh, magnetic particle testing in Pittsburgh, radiographic testing in Pittsburgh and penetrant testing in Pittsburgh, with the weld inspection page covering how D1.1 method work and acceptance decisions divide between NDT technicians and welding inspectors.

sections.heading: How training reaches crews across a three-state basin
paragraphs: Appalachia's workforce is dispersed by nature — crews follow spreads, digs and turnarounds across Pennsylvania, West Virginia and Ohio — so Atlantis delivers training where the crews consolidate, not at fixed premises. The standard models: on-site at the contractor's yard or office, where practical days run on pipe specimens and the crew's own instruments; an arranged venue — a rented training room near the current work — when crews from multiple spreads converge; and blended delivery throughout, with theory completed online between rotations and instructors mobilising only for the practical and examination days.

Scheduling follows the basin's rhythm. Construction examination peaks with the spread season; dig programmes fill the off-season; plant turnarounds cluster in spring and fall. Training slots into the gaps — which is why contractor cohorts are scoped months ahead against the Written Practice, the expected contract requirements and the certification expiry calendar, and why theory-online delivery matters: it is the only component crews can progress while scattered.

sections.heading: Certification and OQ: two systems, one crew
paragraphs: A pipeline NDT technician in this basin answers to two qualification systems at once. Method certification runs under employer-based SNT-TC-1A: the contractor's Written Practice defines training and experience requirements, and a Level III administers general, specific and practical examinations and recommends certification in UT, MT, RT or the method at hand. Operator Qualification runs under PHMSA's rules in 49 CFR 192 and 195: individuals performing covered tasks on regulated pipelines demonstrate task-level qualification through the operators' OQ programmes. Neither substitutes for the other; crews on the right-of-way carry both.

Atlantis NDT supplies the certification side end to end: Written Practice authorship, blended method training, examination administration, and standing outsourced Level III coverage — procedure approval, certification decisions, audit support — for contractors who do not employ a Level III in-house, which in this basin is most of them. Scope is quoted on request against methods, levels, crew size and season. The result the programme is built for: a bench that is certified, current and documented before the spread starts or the dig list lands.

faq.q: Does Atlantis NDT have a training centre in Pittsburgh or the Marcellus?
faq.a: No. Training across Appalachia is delivered on-site at the contractor's yard or facility, or at an arranged venue near where crews consolidate, with theory completed online between rotations and practical days and examinations conducted in person. Atlantis maintains no fixed premises in the region.

faq.q: Does Atlantis sell API 510, 570 or 653 training?
faq.a: No. Atlantis NDT does not offer API 510, API 570 or API 653 certification courses. We train the NDT methods that pipeline, midstream and plant inspection programmes consume — UT, MT, RT, PT, VT and phased array — and provide outsourced Level III services to the contractors and operators running those programmes.

faq.q: Do you offer API 1104 welding inspector or CWI courses?
faq.a: No. API 1104 is the code the basin's girth welds are accepted under, and the AWS CWI credential with its endorsements is the welding-inspector track — neither is an Atlantis product. What we train is the NDT bench that examines welds against API 1104 criteria: conventional UT, RT, MT, and phased array qualification for automated girth-weld systems.

faq.q: Which pages sit inside the Appalachia region?
faq.a: The Pittsburgh training page covers the city market and its method pages (UT, MT, RT, PT); the West Virginia page covers the state; and the oil and gas NDT training page carries the method ladder for the whole vertical.

faq.q: How fast can a contractor field a certified dig crew?
faq.a: The training weeks are short; the schedule driver is the supervised experience the Written Practice requires before Level II certification in each method. Contractors building from experienced-but-uncertified hands move fastest, because documented prior experience counts as the Written Practice allows. Plan cohorts a season ahead — scoped and quoted on request — rather than against a dig list that has already landed.

title: ASNT Level III Basic Exam Guide 2026 | New Reference Editions
description: The ASNT Level III Basic exam changed its reference editions on 1 January 2026: SNT-TC-1A 2024 and CP-189 2024 now apply. 135 questions, 4 hours, closed book — here is exactly what to study.
h1: ASNT Level III Basic Exam Guide 2026: New Reference Editions, Same 135 Questions
answer: Candidates sitting the ASNT NDT Level III Basic exam after 1 January 2026 are tested against the 2024 editions of SNT-TC-1A and ANSI/ASNT CP-189 — the 2020 editions are no longer the exam references. The exam itself is unchanged: 135 multiple-choice questions, 4 hours, closed book, delivered by computer.
expansion: The edition change matters more on the Basic exam than it would on a method exam because roughly a third of the Basic content is certification-program knowledge drawn directly from SNT-TC-1A and CP-189. Questions cite what the current document says — not what a candidate memorized from an older printing. ASNT's Level III Study Guide: Basic was reissued as a 5th edition specifically to align with the 2024 references, so the study guide edition you buy is now as important as the standards themselves.
source: ASNT Certification Services — ASNT NDT Level III examination specifications and recommended references, certification.asnt.org; ASNT Store listings for SNT-TC-1A (2024) and Level III Study Guide: Basic, 5th ed. Verified August 2026.

facets.q: How many questions are on the ASNT Level III Basic exam?
facets.a: The ASNT Level III Basic exam contains 135 equally weighted multiple-choice questions with a 4-hour time limit. It is closed book and delivered by computer. That works out to roughly 1 minute 45 seconds per question, so pacing practice matters as much as content knowledge.

facets.q: Is the ASNT Level III Basic exam open book?
facets.a: No. The Basic exam is closed book — no copies of SNT-TC-1A, CP-189, or personal notes are permitted in the exam room. Candidates must recall requirements language, responsibilities by certification level, and program-administration rules from memory, which is why the edition studied must match the edition tested.

facets.q: What changed for the Basic exam in 2026?
facets.a: Effective 1 January 2026, ASNT replaced the 2020 editions of SNT-TC-1A and ANSI/ASNT CP-189 with the 2024 editions as the exam's recommended references. The question count, time limit, and closed-book format did not change — only the documents the questions are written against.

facets.q: Can I still study from the 2020 edition of SNT-TC-1A?
facets.a: You can, but you will lose questions. The 2024 edition reorganized and updated requirements language, and exam questions reflect the current text. A candidate quoting the 2020 edition's wording or paragraph structure will pick distractors that were written to catch exactly that mismatch.

facets.q: Do I take the Basic exam for every NDT method?
facets.a: No. The Basic exam is taken once. Method exams (UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, and others) are separate examinations sat per method. As long as you hold at least one valid ASNT NDT Level III certificate, you do not repeat the Basic when adding or renewing methods by examination.

facets.q: What score do I need to pass the ASNT Basic exam?
facets.a: ASNT reports Level III results as pass or fail against a criterion-referenced cut score set through its examination-development process; it does not publish a fixed universal percentage for candidates to target. Preparation guidance from experienced Level IIIs is to train to comfortable mastery of the reference documents rather than to a number.

sections.heading: What actually changed on 1 January 2026 — and why it costs points
paragraphs: ASNT's published notice is short and easy to underestimate: for anyone taking the Level III Basic exam after 1 January 2026, the 2020 editions of SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 have been replaced by the 2024 editions as the recommended references. Nothing about the exam's shape changed — still 135 questions, still 4 hours, still closed book. What changed is the text every certification-program question is written against.

The cost shows up in a specific way. Basic exam questions on personnel qualification quote or paraphrase current requirements language: who certifies whom, what an employer's written practice must contain, how examinations are graded and documented, what a Level III is responsible for. When an edition revises a definition or moves a requirement, old-edition answers become well-crafted wrong options. Candidates who prepared thoroughly from the 2020 books routinely report the exam 'felt off' — it wasn't off, it was current.

The practical rule for 2026 candidates: buy or borrow the 2024 editions of both documents before opening a question bank. Question banks and flashcard decks circulating online were mostly built against 2016 and 2020 editions, and rehearsing superseded answers is worse than not rehearsing at all.

sections.heading: Exam mechanics: 135 questions, 4 hours, closed book — and the pacing math
paragraphs: The ASNT Level III Basic exam gives you 240 minutes for 135 equally weighted multiple-choice questions — a shade under 1 minute 45 seconds each. Experienced candidates describe the time pressure as moderate but real: recall questions on SNT-TC-1A responsibilities take 30 seconds, while materials-and-processes questions involving a scenario can absorb three minutes. Banking time on the fast questions is the strategy, not splitting time evenly.

Closed book means genuinely closed: no standards, no formula sheets, no notes. The computer-based format allows flagging and returning to questions, so a first pass answering everything you know cold, followed by a second pass on flagged items, uses the format to full advantage. Because all 135 questions carry equal weight, an unanswered hard question costs exactly as much as an unanswered easy one — never leave blanks.

One structural fact removes a common anxiety: the Basic is sat once per career, not once per method. Pass it, add method exams as your scope grows, and you never see it again — unless certification is allowed to lapse entirely, in which case ASNT treats you as a new candidate and the Basic returns to the schedule. That expiry cliff is covered in our companion guide to Level III recertification points.

sections.heading: What the Basic exam actually tests: three knowledge territories
paragraphs: The Basic exam content splits into three broad territories, and they reward different kinds of preparation. The first is certification-program knowledge: SNT-TC-1A, CP-189, and the structure of qualification and certification itself — training and experience recommendations, examination administration, responsibilities of Level I, II, and III personnel, and what belongs in an employer's written practice. This territory is pure document knowledge, and it is where the 2024 edition change bites.

The second territory is materials, fabrication, and process technology: how discontinuities originate in castings, forgings, welds, and rolled products; heat treatment; mechanical properties; and which flaw types each manufacturing process produces. These questions test whether a Level III can reason from process to probable defect — the judgment that method selection depends on. ASNT's Materials and Processes for NDT Technology text is the standard preparation source here.

The third territory is general familiarity with the major NDT methods at roughly a Level II depth of breadth: the physics, capabilities, and limitations of UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET and companion techniques. You are not expected to be a Level III in every method — you are expected to know enough about each to supervise a program that uses them and to recognize when a method is being misapplied.

sections.heading: SNT-TC-1A 2024 versus 2020: study the current text, not a change summary
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice — 'should' language — that employers adapt into a binding written practice. The 2024 edition continues that model, but revised editions of SNT-TC-1A historically adjust definitions, reorganize paragraphs, and tighten wording around examinations, and memorized 2020 paragraph references do not reliably map onto the 2024 text. Rather than working from a second-hand list of changes, the dependable approach is to study the 2024 document itself, cover to cover, with particular attention to definitions and the examination sections.

CP-189 deserves separate respect because it is a different kind of document. Where SNT-TC-1A recommends, ANSI/ASNT CP-189 is an American National Standard — 'shall' language, minimum requirements that cannot be reduced by an employer's written practice. Basic exam questions probe exactly this distinction: what an employer may modify under SNT-TC-1A versus what CP-189 mandates, including its requirement that a certified NDT Level III be involved in specific program functions. Candidates who study both documents side by side, tracking where they diverge, consistently report that comparison questions became easy points.

A worked study tactic: build a two-column table of topics — qualification records, eligibility, examination grading, recertification, interrupted service — and note what each 2024 document says. The act of building the table is the study; the exam rewards knowing which document says what.

sections.heading: A study sequence that fits working inspectors
paragraphs: A preparation sequence that has worked for practicing technicians studying around full-time inspection work: first read SNT-TC-1A 2024 and CP-189 2024 in full — they are short documents, and a complete read takes an evening each. Second, work through the ASNT Level III Study Guide: Basic, 5th edition, which is aligned to the 2024 references and flags the concepts ASNT considers examinable. Third, spend the longest block on materials and processes, because it is the largest body of content and the least familiar to inspectors who came up through a single method.

Only after those three passes should question banks enter the picture, and then only as a diagnostic — identifying weak territories to re-read, not as the primary learning tool. Most freely circulating Basic question sets predate the 2024 editions, so treat any question about program requirements with suspicion and verify the answer against the current text before accepting it.

We maintain a fuller week-by-week preparation plan, including how to split hours across the three territories, in our ASNT Level III study guide resource — it pairs with this exam-mechanics guide and is updated for the 2026 reference editions.

sections.heading: Eligibility and application: get the experience documentation right first
paragraphs: Eligibility for the ASNT NDT Level III examinations rests on a sliding scale of formal education and NDT experience: more accredited engineering or science education means fewer required years of experience in an assignment comparable to Level II, and candidates with no post-secondary education qualify through additional years of experience alone. ASNT verifies this at application, so the exact current combinations should be read from ASNT's published eligibility criteria rather than from any secondary source, including this one.

The application itself fails candidates more often than the eligibility rules do. Experience must be documented — employer attestations covering dates, methods, and the level of responsibility — and gaps or vague descriptions trigger requests for clarification that can push a candidate past their intended exam window. Assemble the employment evidence before paying the exam fee, and have a current or former supervisor confirm they will attest to it.

Book the exam only after the 2024-edition study materials are in hand. A common and expensive pattern in 2026: candidates who scheduled early against a 2020-edition study plan, then discovered the reference change with weeks to go. The exam date should serve the preparation, not the reverse.

sections.heading: After the Basic: method exams, and where a corporate Level III program comes in
paragraphs: Passing the Basic unlocks nothing by itself — ASNT NDT Level III certification in a method requires the Basic plus that method's examination. Most candidates sit the Basic and their first method exam in the same period while the study momentum holds. Each additional method later is a method exam only, which is why experienced Level IIIs accumulate methods over a career at relatively low marginal effort.

For employers, a newly certified Level III is the beginning of a program, not the end. Someone must translate SNT-TC-1A 2024 into a compliant written practice, build method examinations, keep qualification records audit-ready, and administer Level I and II certification — and the 2024 edition change means every written practice referencing the 2020 edition is now due for revision. Companies without a full-time Level III routinely outsource exactly this function.

Atlantis provides outsourced ASNT Level III services — written practice development to the 2024 editions, examination administration and oversight, and certification-program audits — for inspection companies and asset owners in the US and internationally. The service is affordable, accessible, and fully customizable to your written practice; details and a quote are available on request through our NDT Level III exam oversight consulting page.

faq.q: When did the ASNT Basic exam references change to the 2024 editions?
faq.a: For all Basic exams taken after 1 January 2026, ASNT lists the 2024 editions of SNT-TC-1A and ANSI/ASNT CP-189 as the recommended references, replacing the 2020 editions. Candidates who sat the exam in 2025 were still tested against the 2020 editions.

faq.q: How long is ASNT Level III certification valid, and what if it expires?
faq.a: ASNT NDT Level III certification runs on a five-year (60-month) cycle, renewable by points or by re-examination of the method exams. If certification is allowed to lapse past its expiration date, ASNT requires reapplying as a new candidate — including re-sitting the Basic exam — which makes on-time renewal far cheaper than recovery.

faq.q: Is the ASNT Level III Basic exam harder than the method exams?
faq.a: Most candidates report the Basic as broader but shallower: it demands working knowledge of certification documents, materials and process technology, and every major NDT method, while a method exam demands depth in one. Inspectors from a single-method background usually find materials and processes the hardest territory, not the method questions.

faq.q: Which study guide edition matches the 2026 Basic exam?
faq.a: The ASNT Level III Study Guide: Basic, 5th edition, which is aligned to the 2024 editions of SNT-TC-1A, CP-189, and the CP-105 topical outlines. The 4th edition tracks the superseded 2020 references and will teach answers the 2026 exam no longer accepts.

faq.q: Does Atlantis run ASNT Level III exam preparation?
faq.a: Atlantis provides NDT training through Level III and outsourced Level III consulting, including written practice development to the 2024 editions and examination oversight. We do not administer the ASNT exams themselves — those are booked directly with ASNT — but we prepare candidates and build the employer-side program around them. Quotes on request.

title: ASNT Level III Recertification Points: The 25-Point System Explained
description: ASNT Level III renewal needs 25 points over 60 months — but most rejected applications fail on documentation, not points. Every category, cap, and evidence requirement, plus the points-vs-exam decision.
h1: ASNT Level III Recertification Points: How the 25-Point Renewal Actually Works
answer: ASNT NDT Level III renewal by points requires a minimum of 25 points earned during the five-year (60-month) certification period, documented activity by activity, plus evidence of active NDT employment performing Level III functions for at least 36 months of that period per method being renewed.
expansion: Every point category carries its own evidence requirement and its own cap, so a compliant application is assembled, not remembered. ASNT audits renewal records, and its Certification Management Council makes the final call on questionable documentation — which means the standard to write to is a QA auditor's, not a résumé's. Level IIIs who keep a running evidence folder from year one of the cycle renew in an afternoon; those who reconstruct five years of activity in the final 60 days are the ones who end up re-sitting method exams instead.
source: ASNT Certification Services — Recertification point categories, structure, and documentation requirements; ASNT NDT Level III recertification requirements, certification.asnt.org. Verified August 2026.
